**Louise Elisabeth Glück** ([/ɡ l ɪ k/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_GLIK_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key");[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-2) April 22, 1943 – October 13, 2023) was an American poet and essayist. She won the [2020 Nobel Prize in Literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "2020 Nobel Prize in Literature"), whose judges praised "her unmistakable poetic voice that with austere beauty makes individual existence universal".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-nobel-3) Her other awards include the [Pulitzer Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize_for_Poetry "Pulitzer Prize for Poetry"), [National Humanities Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Humanities_Medal "National Humanities Medal"), [National Book Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Book_Award_for_Poetry "National Book Award for Poetry"), [National Book Critics Circle Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Book_Critics_Circle_Award "National Book Critics Circle Award"), and [Bollingen Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bollingen_Prize "Bollingen Prize"). From 2003 to 2004, she was [Poet Laureate of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poet_Laureate_of_the_United_States "Poet Laureate of the United States").

Glück was born in New York City and raised on [Long Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island "Long Island"). She began to suffer from [anorexia nervosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anorexia_nervosa "Anorexia nervosa") while in high school and later overcame the illness. She attended [Sarah Lawrence College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Lawrence_College "Sarah Lawrence College") and [Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University") but did not obtain a degree. In addition to being an author, she taught poetry at several academic institutions.

Glück is often described as an autobiographical poet; her work is known for its emotional intensity and for frequently drawing on [mythology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mythology "Mythology") or nature imagery to meditate on personal experiences and [modern life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernity "Modernity"). Thematically, her poems have illuminated aspects of [trauma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychological_trauma "Psychological trauma"), desire, and nature. In doing so, they have become known for frank expressions of sadness and [isolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_isolation "Social isolation"). Scholars have also focused on her construction of poetic personas and the relationship, in her poems, between autobiography and classical myth.

Glück served as the Frederick Iseman Professor in the Practice of Poetry at [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University") and as a professor of English at [Stanford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University "Stanford University"). She split her time between [Cambridge, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts "Cambridge, Massachusetts"); [Montpelier, Vermont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montpelier,_Vermont "Montpelier, Vermont"); and [Berkeley, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkeley,_California "Berkeley, California").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-:0-6)

## Life and career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Louise_Gl%C3%BCck&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life and career")]

### Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Louise_Gl%C3%BCck&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early life")]

Louise Glück was born in New York City on April 22, 1943. She was the elder of two surviving daughters of Daniel Glück, a businessman, and Beatrice Glück (née Grosby), a homemaker.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-Morris-2006-7)

Glück's mother was of [Russian Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Jew "Russian Jew") descent.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-Morris-2006-3-8) Her paternal grandparents, Terézia (née Moskovitz) and Henrik Glück, were [Hungarian Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungarian_Jews "Hungarian Jews") from [Érmihályfalva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89rmih%C3%A1lyfalva "Érmihályfalva"), [Bihar County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bihar_County "Bihar County"), in what was then the [Kingdom of Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hungary "Kingdom of Hungary"), [Austro-Hungarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austro-Hungarian_Empire "Austro-Hungarian Empire") (present-day Romania); her grandfather ran a timber company called "Feldmann és Glück".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-10) They emigrated to the United States in December 1900 and eventually owned a grocery store in New York.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-Morris-2006-3-8) Glück's father, who was born in the United States, had an ambition to become a writer, but went into business with his brother-in-law.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-11) Together, they achieved success when they invented the [X-Acto knife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X-Acto "X-Acto").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-Weeks-2003-12) Glück's mother was a graduate of [Wellesley College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wellesley_College "Wellesley College"). In her childhood, Glück's parents taught her [Greek mythology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") and classic stories such as the life of [Joan of Arc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Arc "Joan of Arc").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-13) She began to write poetry at an early age.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-14)

As a teenager, Glück developed [anorexia nervosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anorexia_nervosa "Anorexia nervosa"),[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-Weeks-2003-12)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-Garner-2012-15) which became the defining challenge of her late teenage and young adult years. She described the illness, in one essay, as the result of an effort to assert her independence from her mother.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-Gl%C3%BCck-16) Elsewhere, she connected her illness to the death of an elder sister, an event that occurred before she was born.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-Morris-2006-7) During the fall of her senior year at [George W. Hewlett High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Hewlett_High_School "George W. Hewlett High School"), in [Hewlett, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hewlett,_New_York "Hewlett, New York"), she began [psychoanalytic treatment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychoanalysis "Psychoanalysis"). A few months later, she was taken out of school in order to focus on her rehabilitation, although she still graduated in 1961.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-17) Of that decision, she wrote, "I understood that at some point I was going to die. What I knew more vividly, more viscerally, was that I did not want to die".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-Gl%C3%BCck-16) She spent the next seven years in therapy, which she credited with helping her to overcome the illness and teaching her how to think.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-18)

As a result of her condition, Glück did not enroll in college as a full-time student. She described her decision to forgo higher education in favor of therapy as necessary: "… my emotional condition, my extreme rigidity of behavior and frantic dependence on ritual made other forms of education impossible".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-19) Instead, she took a poetry class at Sarah Lawrence College and, from 1963 to 1966, she enrolled in poetry workshops at [Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University")'s [School of General Studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University_School_of_General_Studies "Columbia University School of General Studies"), which offered courses for non-degree students.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-Haralson-2014-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-22) While there, she studied with [Léonie Adams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9onie_Adams "Léonie Adams") and [Stanley Kunitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Kunitz "Stanley Kunitz"). She credited these teachers as significant mentors in her development as a poet.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-23)

### Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Louise_Gl%C3%BCck&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Career")]

While attending poetry workshops, Glück began to publish her poems. Her first publication was in _[Mademoiselle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mademoiselle\_(magazine) "Mademoiselle (magazine)")_, followed soon after by poems in _[Poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poetry\_(magazine) "Poetry (magazine)")_, _[The New Yorker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_Yorker "The New Yorker")_, _[The Atlantic Monthly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Atlantic "The Atlantic")_, _[The Nation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Nation "The Nation")_, and other venues.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-25) After leaving Columbia, Glück supported herself with secretarial work.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-National_Endowment_for_the_Humanities_(NEH)-26) She married Charles Hertz Jr. in 1967.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-Morris-2006-2-27) In 1968, Glück published her first collection of poems, _Firstborn_, which received some positive critical attention. In a review, the poet [Robert Hass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Hass "Robert Hass") described the book as "hard, artful, and full of pain".[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-28) However, reflecting on it in 2003, the critic [Stephanie Burt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Burt "Stephanie Burt") said the collection "revealed a forceful but clotted poet, an anxious imitator of [Robert Lowell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Lowell "Robert Lowell") and [Sylvia Plath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvia_Plath "Sylvia Plath")".[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-29) Following the publication, Glück experienced a prolonged case of [writer's block](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Writer's_block "Writer's block"), which was not cured, she said, until 1971, when she began to teach poetry at [Goddard College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goddard_College "Goddard College") in Vermont.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-National_Endowment_for_the_Humanities_(NEH)-26)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-30) The poems she wrote during this time were collected in her second book, _The House on Marshland_ (1975), which many critics have regarded as her breakthrough work, signaling her "discovery of a distinctive voice".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-Morris-31)

In 1973, Glück gave birth to her son, Noah, with her partner, Keith Monley, who helped raise him for the first two years of his life.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-Weeks-2003-12)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-32) Her marriage to Charles Hertz, Jr. had ended in divorce, and in 1977 she married John Dranow, an author who had started the summer writing program at Goddard College.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-Morris-2006-2-27)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-Flagg-33) In 1980, Dranow and Francis Voigt, the husband of poet [Ellen Bryant Voigt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellen_Bryant_Voigt "Ellen Bryant Voigt"), co-founded the [New England Culinary Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England_Culinary_Institute "New England Culinary Institute") as a private, for-profit college. Glück and Bryant Voigt were early investors in the institute and served on its board of directors.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-Flagg-33)

In 1980, Glück's third collection, _Descending Figure_, was published. It received some criticism for its tone and subject matter: for example, the poet [Greg Kuzma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greg_Kuzma "Greg Kuzma") accused Glück of being a "child hater" for her now anthologized poem, "The Drowned Children".[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-34) On the whole, however, the book was well received. In _[The American Poetry Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_American\_Poetry\_Review "The American Poetry Review")_, [Mary Kinzie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Kinzie "Mary Kinzie") praised the book's illumination of "deprived, harmed, stammering beings".[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-35) Writing in _Poetry_, the poet and critic [J. D. McClatchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._D._McClatchy "J. D. McClatchy") said the book was "a considerable advance on Glück's previous work" and "one of the year's outstanding books".[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-36) That same year, a fire destroyed Glück's house in Vermont, resulting in the loss of most of her possessions.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-Morris-2006-2-27)

In the wake of that tragedy, Glück began to write the poems that would later be collected in her award-winning work, _[The Triumph of Achilles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Triumph\_of\_Achilles "The Triumph of Achilles")_ (1985). Writing in _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_, the author and critic [Liz Rosenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liz_Rosenberg "Liz Rosenberg") described the collection as "clearer, purer, and sharper" than Glück's previous work.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-37) The critic Peter Stitt, writing in _[The Georgia Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Georgia\_Review "The Georgia Review")_, declared that the book showed Glück to be "among the important poets of our age".[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-38) From the collection, the poem "Mock Orange", which has been likened to a feminist anthem,[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-39) has been called an "anthology piece" because of its frequent inclusion in poetry anthologies and college courses.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-Hahn-2004-40)

In 1984, Glück joined the faculty of [Williams College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Williams_College "Williams College") in Massachusetts as a senior lecturer in the English Department.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-41) The following year, her father died.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-42) The loss prompted her to begin a new collection of poems, _Ararat_ (1990), the title of which references the mountain of the [Genesis flood narrative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genesis_flood_narrative "Genesis flood narrative"). Writing in _The New York Times_ in 2012, the critic [Dwight Garner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwight_Garner_(critic) "Dwight Garner (critic)") called it "the most brutal and sorrow-filled book of American poetry published in the last 25 years".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-Garner-2012-15) Glück followed this collection with one of her most popular and critically acclaimed books, _[The Wild Iris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Wild\_Iris "The Wild Iris")_ (1992), which features garden flowers in conversation with a gardener and a deity about the nature of life. _[Publishers Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers\_Weekly "Publishers Weekly")_ proclaimed it an "important book" that showcased "poetry of great beauty".[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-43) The critic Elizabeth Lund, writing in _The_ _[Christian Science Monitor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian\_Science\_Monitor "Christian Science Monitor")_, called it "a milestone work".[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-44) It went on to win the Pulitzer Prize in 1993, cementing Glück's reputation as a preeminent American poet.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-45)

While the 1990s brought Glück literary success, it was also a period of personal hardship. In 1996 her marriage to John Dranow ended in divorce, the difficult nature of which affected their business relationship, resulting in Dranow's removal from his positions at the New England Culinary Institute.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-Flagg-33)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-46) Glück channeled her experience into her writing, entering a prolific period of her career. In 1994, she published a collection of essays called _Proofs & Theories: Essays on Poetry_. She then produced _Meadowlands_ (1996), a collection of poetry about the nature of love and the deterioration of a marriage.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-47) She followed it with two more collections: _Vita Nova_ (1999) and _The Seven Ages_ (2001).

In 2004, in response to the [terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks "September 11 attacks"), Glück published a [chapbook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapbook "Chapbook") entitled _October_. Consisting of one poem divided into six parts, it draws on ancient Greek myth to explore aspects of trauma and suffering.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-48) That same year, she was named the Rosenkranz Writer in Residence at Yale University.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-49)

After joining the faculty of Yale, Glück continued to publish poetry. Her books published during this period include _Averno_ (2006), _A Village Life_ (2009), and _[Faithful and Virtuous Night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faithful\_and\_Virtuous\_Night "Faithful and Virtuous Night")_ (2014). In 2012, the publication of a collection of a half-century's worth of her poems, entitled _Poems: 1962–2012_, was called "a literary event".[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-50) Another collection of her essays, entitled _American Originality_, appeared in 2017.

In October 2020, Glück was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, becoming the sixteenth female literature laureate since the prize was founded in 1901.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-51) Due to restrictions caused by the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), she received her prize at her home.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-52) In her Nobel lecture, which was delivered in writing, she highlighted her early engagement with poetry by [William Blake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Blake "William Blake") and [Emily Dickinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emily_Dickinson "Emily Dickinson") in discussing the relationship between poets, readers, and the wider public.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-53)

In 2021, Glück's collection, _Winter Recipes from the Collective_, was published. In 2022, she was named the Frederick Iseman Professor in the Practice of Poetry at Yale.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-54) In 2023, she was appointed a professor of English at Stanford University, where she taught in the Creative Writing Program.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-:0-6)

### Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Louise_Gl%C3%BCck&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Glück's elder sister died young before Glück was born. Her younger sister, Tereze (1945–2018), worked at [Citibank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citibank "Citibank") as a vice president and was also a writer, winning the [Iowa Short Fiction Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iowa_Short_Fiction_Award "Iowa Short Fiction Award") in 1995 for her book, _May You Live in Interesting Times_.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-55) Glück's niece is the actress [Abigail Savage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abigail_Savage "Abigail Savage").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-56)

She remained a close confidant and friend to Vermont novelist [Kathryn Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathryn_Davis_(writer) "Kathryn Davis (writer)") throughout her life. The two often corresponded to share their developing works, seeking creative advice throughout their lengthy friendship and writing careers.

Glück died from cancer at home in [Cambridge, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts "Cambridge, Massachusetts"), on October 13, 2023, at age 80.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-Risen-57)

Glück's work has been the subject of academic study. Her papers, including manuscripts, correspondence, and other materials, are housed at the [Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beinecke_Rare_Book_&_Manuscript_Library "Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library") at Yale University.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-58)

### Form

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Louise_Gl%C3%BCck&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Form")]

Glück is best known for lyric poems of linguistic precision and dark tone. The poet [Craig Morgan Teicher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craig_Morgan_Teicher "Craig Morgan Teicher") has described her as a writer for whom "words are always scarce, hard won, and not to be wasted".[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-59) The scholar Laura Quinney has argued that her careful use of words put Glück into "the line of American poets who value fierce lyric compression", from [Emily Dickinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emily_Dickinson "Emily Dickinson") to [Elizabeth Bishop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Bishop "Elizabeth Bishop").[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-Quinney-2005-60) Glück's poems shifted in form throughout her career, beginning with short, terse lyrics composed of compact lines and expanding into connected book-length sequences.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-61) Her work is not known for poetic techniques such as rhyme or alliteration. Rather, the poet Robert Hahn has called her style "radically inconspicuous" or "virtually an absence of style", relying on a voice that blends "portentous intonations" with a conversational approach.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-Hahn-2004-40)

Among scholars and reviewers, there has been discussion as to whether Glück is a [confessional poet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confessional_poetry "Confessional poetry"), owing to the prevalence of the first-person mode in her poems and their intimate subject matter, often inspired by events in Glück's personal life. The scholar Robert Baker has argued that Glück "is surely a confessional poet in some basic sense",[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-62) while the critic Michael Robbins has argued that Glück's poetry, unlike that of confessional poets [Sylvia Plath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvia_Plath "Sylvia Plath") or [John Berryman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Berryman "John Berryman"), "depends upon the fiction of privacy".[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-Robbins-2012-63) In other words, she cannot be a confessional poet, Robbins argues, if she does not address an audience. Going further, Quinney argues that, to Glück, the confessional poem is "odious".[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-Quinney-2005-60) Others have noted that Glück's poems can be viewed as autobiographical, while her technique of inhabiting various personas, ranging from ancient Greek gods to garden flowers, renders her poems more than mere confessions. As the scholar [Helen Vendler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helen_Vendler "Helen Vendler") has noted: "In their obliquity and reserve, [Glück's poems] offer an alternative to first-person 'confession', while remaining indisputably personal".[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-64)

### Themes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Louise_Gl%C3%BCck&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Themes")]

While Glück's work is thematically diverse, scholars and critics have identified several themes that are paramount. Most prominently, Glück's poetry can be said to focus on trauma, as she wrote throughout her career about death, loss, suffering, failed relationships, and attempts at healing and renewal.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-65) The scholar Daniel Morris notes that even a Glück poem that uses traditionally happy or idyllic imagery "suggests the author's awareness of mortality, of the loss of innocence".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-Morris-31) The scholar Joanne Feit Diehl echoes this notion when she argues that "this 'sense of an ending' … infuses Glück's poems with their retrospective power", pointing to her transformation of common objects, such as a baby stroller, into representations of loneliness and loss.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-66) Yet, for Glück, trauma was arguably a gateway to a greater appreciation of life, a concept explored in _The Triumph of Achilles_. The triumph to which the title alludes is Achilles' acceptance of mortality—which enables him to become a more fully realized human being.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-67)

Another of Glück's common themes is desire. Glück wrote directly about many forms of desire—for example, the desire for love or insight—but her approach is marked by ambivalence. Morris argues that Glück's poems, which often adopt contradictory points of view, reflect "her own ambivalent relationship to status, power, morality, gender, and, most of all, language".[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-68) The author Robert Boyer has characterized Glück's ambivalence as a result of "strenuous self-interrogation". He argues that "Glück's poems at their best have always moved between recoil and affirmation, sensuous immediacy and reflection … for a poet who can often seem earthbound and defiantly unillusioned, she has been powerfully responsive to the lure of the daily miracle and the sudden upsurge of overmastering emotion".[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-69) The tension between competing desires in Glück's work manifests both in her assumption of different personas from poem to poem and in her varied approach to each collection of her poems. This led the poet and scholar [James Longenbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Longenbach "James Longenbach") to declare that "change is Louise Glück's highest value" and "if change is what she most craves, it is also what she most resists, what is most difficult for her, most hard-won".[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-70)

Another of Glück's preoccupations was nature, the setting for many of her poems. In _The Wild Iris_, the poems take place in a garden where flowers have intelligent, emotive voices. However, Morris points out that _The House on Marshland_ is also concerned with nature and can be read as a revision of the [Romantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romantic_poetry "Romantic poetry") tradition of nature poetry.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-71) In _Ararat_, too, "flowers become a language of mourning", useful for both commemoration and competition among mourners to determine the "ownership of nature as a meaningful system of symbolism".[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-72) Thus, in Glück's work nature is both something to be regarded critically and embraced. The author and critic Alan Williamson has said it can also sometimes suggest the divine, as when, in the poem "Celestial Music", the speaker states that "when you love the world you hear celestial music", or when, in "The Wild Iris", the deity speaks through changes in weather.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-73)

Glück's poetry is also notable for what it avoids. Morris argues that

> Glück's writing most often evades ethnic identification, religious classification, or gendered affiliation. In fact, her poetry often negates critical assessments that affirm [identity politics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Identity_politics "Identity politics") as criteria for literary evaluation. She resists [canonization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canon_(basic_principle) "Canon (basic principle)") as a hyphenated poet (that is, as a "Jewish-American" poet, or a "feminist" poet, or a "nature" poet), preferring instead to retain an aura of [iconoclasm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iconoclasm "Iconoclasm"), or in-betweenness.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-74)

### Influences

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Louise_Gl%C3%BCck&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Influences")]

Glück pointed to the influence of [psychoanalysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychoanalysis "Psychoanalysis") on her work, as well as her early learning in ancient legends, parables, and mythology. In addition, she credited the influence of Léonie Adams and Stanley Kunitz. Scholars and critics have pointed to the literary influence on her work of [Robert Lowell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Lowell "Robert Lowell"),[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-75)[Rainer Maria Rilke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainer_Maria_Rilke "Rainer Maria Rilke"),[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-Robbins-2012-63) and [Emily Dickinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emily_Dickinson "Emily Dickinson"),[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-76) among others.

### Elected or invited posts

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Louise_Gl%C3%BCck&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Elected or invited posts")]

In 1999, Glück, along with the poets [Rita Dove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rita_Dove "Rita Dove") and [W. S. Merwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._S._Merwin "W. S. Merwin"), was asked to serve as a special consultant to the [Library of Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Congress "Library of Congress") for that institution's bicentennial. In this capacity, she helped the Library of Congress to determine programming to mark its 200th anniversary celebration.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-115) In 1999, she was also elected a Chancellor of the [Academy of American Poets](https://poets.org/), a post she held until 2005.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-116) In 2003, she was appointed the judge of the [Yale Series of Younger Poets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_Series_of_Younger_Poets "Yale Series of Younger Poets"), a position she held until 2010. The Yale Series is the oldest annual literary competition in the United States, and during her time as judge, she selected for publication works by the poets [Jay Hopler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jay_Hopler "Jay Hopler"), [Peter Streckfus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Streckfus "Peter Streckfus"), and [Fady Joudah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fady_Joudah "Fady Joudah"), among others.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-117)

Glück was a visiting faculty member at many institutions, including [Stanford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University "Stanford University"),[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-118)[Boston University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_University "Boston University"),[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-119) the [University of North Carolina, Greensboro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_North_Carolina_at_Greensboro "University of North Carolina at Greensboro"),[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-120) and the [Iowa Writers Workshop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iowa_Writers'_Workshop "Iowa Writers' Workshop").[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louise_Gl%C3%BCck#cite_note-121)

Field of British literature

**British poetry** is the field of [British literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_literature "British literature") encompassing [poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poetry "Poetry") from anywhere in the British world – whether of the [British Isles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Isles "British Isles"), the [British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire"), or the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom").

## Types

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=British_poetry&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Types")]

*   [English poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_poetry "English poetry")
*   [Irish poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_poetry "Irish poetry") from Northern Ireland
*   [Scottish poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_poetry "Scottish poetry") (see _[Scottish literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish\_literature "Scottish literature")_)
*   [Welsh poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welsh_poetry "Welsh poetry")
*   [Jèrriais poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%A8rriais_literature "Jèrriais literature")
*   [Guernésiais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guern%C3%A9siais "Guernésiais") poetry
*   [Manx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manx_literature "Manx literature") poetry
*   [Cornish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornish_literature "Cornish literature") poetry

## Women poets

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=British_poetry&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Women poets")]

The critic Lyn Pykett has written that "A trawl through anthologies of British or English verse quickly discovers the exclusion of women from the traditions of British poetry".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poetry_of_the_United_Kingdom#cite_note-Pykett-1)

**Adrienne Raphel** (born 1988) is an American poet and writer. She has published works of poetry as well as a book on the history of [crossword puzzles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossword "Crossword").

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Adrienne_Raphel&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Raphel was born in New Jersey but grew up in [St. Johnsbury, Vermont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Johnsbury,_Vermont "St. Johnsbury, Vermont"), from age ten.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Raphel#cite_note-SJA23-1) She attended the private school [St. Johnsbury Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Johnsbury_Academy "St. Johnsbury Academy"), writing a puzzle pamphlet as a capstone project in her senior year in 2006.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Raphel#cite_note-SJA23-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Raphel#cite_note-LARB-2) She earned her [Bachelor of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") from [Princeton University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton_University "Princeton University") in 2010, [Master of Fine Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Fine_Arts "Master of Fine Arts") in poetry from the [Iowa Writers' Workshop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iowa_Writers'_Workshop "Iowa Writers' Workshop"), and [PhD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Philosophy "Doctor of Philosophy") in English from [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Raphel#cite_note-SJA23-1)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Adrienne_Raphel&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Raphel has written for _[The New Yorker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_Yorker "The New Yorker")_, _[The Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Atlantic "The Atlantic")_, and _[The Paris Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Paris\_Review "The Paris Review")_.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Raphel#cite_note-SD18-3) Her first poetry collection, _What Was It For_, was published by Rescue Press in 2017; two years before, the manuscript won the publisher's Black Box Poetry Prize contest.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Raphel#cite_note-SD18-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Raphel#cite_note-4) Her collection _Our Dark Academia_ (2022) contains poetry and prose about modern life, including a parody [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia "Wikipedia") article on what she calls "dark academia".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Raphel#cite_note-CRB23-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Raphel#cite_note-6)

Raphel writes about the history of [crossword puzzles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossword "Crossword") in _Thinking Inside the Box_ (2020), published by [Penguin Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penguin_Group "Penguin Group"). The book grew out of her PhD dissertation on crosswords.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Raphel#cite_note-LARB-2)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Raphel#cite_note-CRB23-5) Besides conducting archival research and interviews, she competed in the [American Crossword Puzzle Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Crossword_Puzzle_Tournament "American Crossword Puzzle Tournament") and submitted her own puzzle to _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times\_crossword\_puzzle "The New York Times crossword puzzle")_.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Raphel#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Raphel#cite_note-8)

**Adrienne Raphel** (born 1988) is an American poet and writer. She has published works of poetry as well as a book on the history of [crossword puzzles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossword "Crossword").

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Adrienne_Raphel&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Raphel was born in New Jersey but grew up in [St. Johnsbury, Vermont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Johnsbury,_Vermont "St. Johnsbury, Vermont"), from age ten.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Raphel#cite_note-SJA23-1) She attended the private school [St. Johnsbury Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Johnsbury_Academy "St. Johnsbury Academy"), writing a puzzle pamphlet as a capstone project in her senior year in 2006.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Raphel#cite_note-SJA23-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Raphel#cite_note-LARB-2) She earned her [Bachelor of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") from [Princeton University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton_University "Princeton University") in 2010, [Master of Fine Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Fine_Arts "Master of Fine Arts") in poetry from the [Iowa Writers' Workshop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iowa_Writers'_Workshop "Iowa Writers' Workshop"), and [PhD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Philosophy "Doctor of Philosophy") in English from [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Raphel#cite_note-SJA23-1)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Adrienne_Raphel&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Raphel has written for _[The New Yorker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_Yorker "The New Yorker")_, _[The Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Atlantic "The Atlantic")_, and _[The Paris Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Paris\_Review "The Paris Review")_.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Raphel#cite_note-SD18-3) Her first poetry collection, _What Was It For_, was published by Rescue Press in 2017; two years before, the manuscript won the publisher's Black Box Poetry Prize contest.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Raphel#cite_note-SD18-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Raphel#cite_note-4) Her collection _Our Dark Academia_ (2022) contains poetry and prose about modern life, including a parody [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia "Wikipedia") article on what she calls "dark academia".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Raphel#cite_note-CRB23-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Raphel#cite_note-6)

Raphel writes about the history of [crossword puzzles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crossword "Crossword") in _Thinking Inside the Box_ (2020), published by [Penguin Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penguin_Group "Penguin Group"). The book grew out of her PhD dissertation on crosswords.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Raphel#cite_note-LARB-2)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Raphel#cite_note-CRB23-5) Besides conducting archival research and interviews, she competed in the [American Crossword Puzzle Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Crossword_Puzzle_Tournament "American Crossword Puzzle Tournament") and submitted her own puzzle to _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times\_crossword\_puzzle "The New York Times crossword puzzle")_.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Raphel#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrienne_Raphel#cite_note-8)

**Marie Howe** (born 1950) is an American poet. Howe served as [New York Poet Laureate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poets_Laureate_of_New_York "Poets Laureate of New York") from 2012–2016. She is currently a Chancellor of the [Academy of American Poets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_American_Poets "Academy of American Poets") and Poet-in-Residence at [The Cathedral of St John the Divine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathedral_of_St._John_the_Divine "Cathedral of St. John the Divine"). Throughout her career, she has received fellowships from the [John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Simon_Guggenheim_Memorial_Foundation_Fellowship "John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation Fellowship"), the [National Endowment for the Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Endowment_for_the_Arts "National Endowment for the Arts"), the [Harvard Radcliffe Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Radcliffe_Institute "Harvard Radcliffe Institute"), and [The Fine Arts Work Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fine_Arts_Work_Center "Fine Arts Work Center") in Provincetown.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-1)

In 1987, her debut collection _The Good Thief_ was selected by [Margaret Atwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Atwood "Margaret Atwood") for the [National Poetry Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Poetry_Series "National Poetry Series").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-:0-2) Her subsequent collections include _What the Living Do_ (1997), _The Kingdom of Ordinary Time_ (2008), and _Magdalene_ (2017), which was Longlisted for the [National Book Award for Poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Book_Award_for_Poetry "National Book Award for Poetry").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-3) In 2024 [W. W. Norton & Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._W._Norton_&_Company "W. W. Norton & Company") published her _New & Selected Poems_,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-4) while [Bloodaxe Books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloodaxe_Books "Bloodaxe Books") published its UK companion, _What the Earth Seemed to Say_, to critical acclaim.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-5)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Marie_Howe&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Howe was born in [Rochester, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rochester,_New_York "Rochester, New York"). In a 2013 interview with _[On Being](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On\_Being "On Being")_, Howe would note that

> I grew up in the [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church") religion, in a large [Irish-Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Catholics "Irish Catholics") family. I was the oldest daughter out of nine children. All of my sisters had nine or ten kids, and all of my father’s sisters and brothers also had nine or ten kids, so I had literally over a hundred first cousins. It was a tribal childhood, and the Catholicism was at the center of it.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-Howe.OnBeing.2013-6)

In the 1960s, Howe enrolled in the [Academy of the Sacred Heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Schools_of_the_Sacred_Heart "List of Schools of the Sacred Heart"), a socially progressive, [parochial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parochial_school "Parochial school") all-girls school, where the nuns centered what Theology has to do with “social justice, service, questioning, and authority.”[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-Howe.OnBeing.2013-6) Howe would later observe that “it was there that I began to appreciate that spirituality could be rigorous, imaginative and an essential part of living in the physical world.”[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-Howe.OnBeing.2013-6) During this time she would spend “hours lying in the bathtub” reading from _[The Lives of Saints](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alban\_Butler "Alban Butler")_, which would become her first example of “women who were the subjects of their own lives, not objects.”[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-Howe.OnBeing.2013-6)

Howe would later attend the [University of Windsor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor "University of Windsor"), a historically Roman Catholic university in [Ontario, Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario "Ontario"), where she earned a BA degree in English. She would subsequently relocate to [Groton, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groton,_Massachusetts "Groton, Massachusetts"), to pursue a career as a journalist, and later a high school English teacher. In 1980, she received a fellowship to the Summer Humanities Institute at [Dartmouth College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmouth_College "Dartmouth College"), where she had applied to study Philosophy, but ended up enrolling in a creative writing workshop.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-Howe.Believer.2019-7)

In 1981, Howe relocated to [Concord, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concord,_Massachusetts "Concord, Massachusetts"). When reflecting on this time later in life, Howe would note that

> Every day I would walk to the old North Bridge and visit [Thoreau’s Grave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_David_Thoreau "Henry David Thoreau") and [Emerson's grave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Waldo_Emerson "Ralph Waldo Emerson"). I was so lonely, lonely, lonely. And I learned how to sit still. And how to sit in a chair and bang on a typewriter. You know. You have to learn how to sit still. I didn’t know how to do that. It took me a long time. I applied to graduate schools and I went. It was a miracle.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-Howe.Believer.2019-7)

The following year, she moved to [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") to pursue an MFA in Creative Writing at [Columbia University School of the Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University_School_of_the_Arts "Columbia University School of the Arts").

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Marie_Howe&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Howe worked briefly as a newspaper reporter in Rochester and as a high-school English teacher in Massachusetts. She did not devote serious attention to writing poetry until she turned 30. At the suggestion of an instructor in a writers' workshop, Howe applied to and was accepted at [Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University") where she studied with [Stanley Kunitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Kunitz "Stanley Kunitz") and received her M.F.A. in 1983.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-9)

She has taught writing at [Tufts University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tufts_University "Tufts University") and [Warren Wilson College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Wilson_College "Warren Wilson College"). She is presently on the writing faculties at [Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University"), [Sarah Lawrence College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Lawrence_College "Sarah Lawrence College"), and [New York University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_University "New York University").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-11)

Her first book, _The Good Thief_, was selected by [Margaret Atwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Atwood "Margaret Atwood") as the winner of the 1987 Open Competition of the [National Poetry Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Poetry_Series "National Poetry Series").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-12) In 1998, she published her best-known book of poems, _What the Living Do_; the title poem in the collection is a haunting lament for her brother with the plain-spoken last line: "I am living, I remember you."

Howe's brother John died of an [AIDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIDS "AIDS")-related illness in 1989. "John’s living and dying changed my aesthetic entirely," she has said.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-13) In 1995, Howe co-edited, with Michael Klein, a collection of essays, letters, and stories entitled _In the Company of My Solitude: American Writing from the AIDS Pandemic_.

Her poems have appeared in literary journals and magazines including _The New Yorker, The Atlantic, Poetry, Agni, Ploughshares,_ and _Harvard Review._[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-14) Her honors include National Endowment for the Arts and Guggenheim fellowships.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-16)

In January 2018, Howe was elected a Chancellor of the [Academy of American Poets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_American_Poets "Academy of American Poets").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-17)

## Literary themes and style

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Marie_Howe&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Literary themes and style")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/96/Poets_Wash_Square_NYC_Poetry_Rally_December_20%2C_2014_35.jpg/500px-Poets_Wash_Square_NYC_Poetry_Rally_December_20%2C_2014_35.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Poets_Wash_Square_NYC_Poetry_Rally_December_20,_2014_35.jpg)

Howe at New York City Poetry Rally 2014, with [Suzanne Gardinier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suzanne_Gardinier "Suzanne Gardinier")

Marie Howe is praised for her poetry which captures the metaphysical and spiritual dimensions of everyday life.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-:0-2) Her work explores the nature of the soul and the self through literary themes of life, death, love, pain, hope, despair, sin, virtue, solitude, community, impermanence, and the eternal.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-:1-18) Despite the strong themes in her writing, Howe subtly expresses these messages through the explanation of daily tasks and regular lifestyles in most of her poems.

Her first collection, _The Good Thief_ (1988), was made philosophical and reflective with the incorporation of Biblical and mythical allusions. Margaret Atwood, who chose this book for the National Poetry Series, praised Howe’s “poems of obsession that transcend their own dark roots.”[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-:0-2) Additionally, Stanley Kunitz noted, “Her long, deep-breathing lines address the mysteries of flesh and spirit, in terms accessible only to a woman who is very much of our time and yet still in touch with the sacred.” Such an esteemed review justified the selection of _The Good Thief_ for the Lavan Younger Poets Prize from the American Academy of Poets.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-19)

A year after the publication of her first poetry book (1989), Howe’s brother John died from [AIDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIDS "AIDS"). According to Howe in an [AGNI](https://agnionline.bu.edu/about/our-people/authors/marie-howe) interview, “John’s living and dying changed my aesthetic completely.”[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-:0-2) Consequently in 1997, she published a second collection, _What the Living Do_, as an elegy for John which reflected a new style. Stripped of metaphors, her writing was described as “a transparent, accessible documentary of loss” by the [Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/marie-howe).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-:0-2)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-:1-18)

In 2008, Howe distanced herself from the personal narrative and returned to the spiritual style in _The Kingdom of Ordinary Time_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-:0-2) This is most representative of Howe’s style now, a balance between the ordinary and unordinary. It is best put by playwright Eve Ensler, who describes her poems as “a guide to living on the brink of the mystical and the mundane.”[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-:1-18)

**Marie Howe** (born 1950) is an American poet. Howe served as [New York Poet Laureate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poets_Laureate_of_New_York "Poets Laureate of New York") from 2012–2016. She is currently a Chancellor of the [Academy of American Poets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_American_Poets "Academy of American Poets") and Poet-in-Residence at [The Cathedral of St John the Divine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathedral_of_St._John_the_Divine "Cathedral of St. John the Divine"). Throughout her career, she has received fellowships from the [John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Simon_Guggenheim_Memorial_Foundation_Fellowship "John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation Fellowship"), the [National Endowment for the Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Endowment_for_the_Arts "National Endowment for the Arts"), the [Harvard Radcliffe Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Radcliffe_Institute "Harvard Radcliffe Institute"), and [The Fine Arts Work Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fine_Arts_Work_Center "Fine Arts Work Center") in Provincetown.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-1)

In 1987, her debut collection _The Good Thief_ was selected by [Margaret Atwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Atwood "Margaret Atwood") for the [National Poetry Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Poetry_Series "National Poetry Series").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-:0-2) Her subsequent collections include _What the Living Do_ (1997), _The Kingdom of Ordinary Time_ (2008), and _Magdalene_ (2017), which was Longlisted for the [National Book Award for Poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Book_Award_for_Poetry "National Book Award for Poetry").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-3) In 2024 [W. W. Norton & Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._W._Norton_&_Company "W. W. Norton & Company") published her _New & Selected Poems_,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-4) while [Bloodaxe Books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloodaxe_Books "Bloodaxe Books") published its UK companion, _What the Earth Seemed to Say_, to critical acclaim.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-5)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Marie_Howe&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Howe was born in [Rochester, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rochester,_New_York "Rochester, New York"). In a 2013 interview with _[On Being](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On\_Being "On Being")_, Howe would note that

> I grew up in the [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church") religion, in a large [Irish-Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Catholics "Irish Catholics") family. I was the oldest daughter out of nine children. All of my sisters had nine or ten kids, and all of my father’s sisters and brothers also had nine or ten kids, so I had literally over a hundred first cousins. It was a tribal childhood, and the Catholicism was at the center of it.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-Howe.OnBeing.2013-6)

In the 1960s, Howe enrolled in the [Academy of the Sacred Heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Schools_of_the_Sacred_Heart "List of Schools of the Sacred Heart"), a socially progressive, [parochial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parochial_school "Parochial school") all-girls school, where the nuns centered what Theology has to do with “social justice, service, questioning, and authority.”[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-Howe.OnBeing.2013-6) Howe would later observe that “it was there that I began to appreciate that spirituality could be rigorous, imaginative and an essential part of living in the physical world.”[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-Howe.OnBeing.2013-6) During this time she would spend “hours lying in the bathtub” reading from _[The Lives of Saints](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alban\_Butler "Alban Butler")_, which would become her first example of “women who were the subjects of their own lives, not objects.”[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-Howe.OnBeing.2013-6)

Howe would later attend the [University of Windsor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor "University of Windsor"), a historically Roman Catholic university in [Ontario, Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario "Ontario"), where she earned a BA degree in English. She would subsequently relocate to [Groton, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groton,_Massachusetts "Groton, Massachusetts"), to pursue a career as a journalist, and later a high school English teacher. In 1980, she received a fellowship to the Summer Humanities Institute at [Dartmouth College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dartmouth_College "Dartmouth College"), where she had applied to study Philosophy, but ended up enrolling in a creative writing workshop.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-Howe.Believer.2019-7)

In 1981, Howe relocated to [Concord, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concord,_Massachusetts "Concord, Massachusetts"). When reflecting on this time later in life, Howe would note that

> Every day I would walk to the old North Bridge and visit [Thoreau’s Grave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_David_Thoreau "Henry David Thoreau") and [Emerson's grave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Waldo_Emerson "Ralph Waldo Emerson"). I was so lonely, lonely, lonely. And I learned how to sit still. And how to sit in a chair and bang on a typewriter. You know. You have to learn how to sit still. I didn’t know how to do that. It took me a long time. I applied to graduate schools and I went. It was a miracle.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-Howe.Believer.2019-7)

The following year, she moved to [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") to pursue an MFA in Creative Writing at [Columbia University School of the Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University_School_of_the_Arts "Columbia University School of the Arts").

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Marie_Howe&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Howe worked briefly as a newspaper reporter in Rochester and as a high-school English teacher in Massachusetts. She did not devote serious attention to writing poetry until she turned 30. At the suggestion of an instructor in a writers' workshop, Howe applied to and was accepted at [Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University") where she studied with [Stanley Kunitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Kunitz "Stanley Kunitz") and received her M.F.A. in 1983.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-9)

She has taught writing at [Tufts University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tufts_University "Tufts University") and [Warren Wilson College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warren_Wilson_College "Warren Wilson College"). She is presently on the writing faculties at [Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University"), [Sarah Lawrence College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Lawrence_College "Sarah Lawrence College"), and [New York University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_University "New York University").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-11)

Her first book, _The Good Thief_, was selected by [Margaret Atwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Atwood "Margaret Atwood") as the winner of the 1987 Open Competition of the [National Poetry Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Poetry_Series "National Poetry Series").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-12) In 1998, she published her best-known book of poems, _What the Living Do_; the title poem in the collection is a haunting lament for her brother with the plain-spoken last line: "I am living, I remember you."

Howe's brother John died of an [AIDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIDS "AIDS")-related illness in 1989. "John’s living and dying changed my aesthetic entirely," she has said.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-13) In 1995, Howe co-edited, with Michael Klein, a collection of essays, letters, and stories entitled _In the Company of My Solitude: American Writing from the AIDS Pandemic_.

Her poems have appeared in literary journals and magazines including _The New Yorker, The Atlantic, Poetry, Agni, Ploughshares,_ and _Harvard Review._[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-14) Her honors include National Endowment for the Arts and Guggenheim fellowships.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-16)

In January 2018, Howe was elected a Chancellor of the [Academy of American Poets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_American_Poets "Academy of American Poets").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-17)

## Literary themes and style

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Marie_Howe&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Literary themes and style")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/96/Poets_Wash_Square_NYC_Poetry_Rally_December_20%2C_2014_35.jpg/500px-Poets_Wash_Square_NYC_Poetry_Rally_December_20%2C_2014_35.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Poets_Wash_Square_NYC_Poetry_Rally_December_20,_2014_35.jpg)

Howe at New York City Poetry Rally 2014, with [Suzanne Gardinier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suzanne_Gardinier "Suzanne Gardinier")

Marie Howe is praised for her poetry which captures the metaphysical and spiritual dimensions of everyday life.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-:0-2) Her work explores the nature of the soul and the self through literary themes of life, death, love, pain, hope, despair, sin, virtue, solitude, community, impermanence, and the eternal.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-:1-18) Despite the strong themes in her writing, Howe subtly expresses these messages through the explanation of daily tasks and regular lifestyles in most of her poems.

Her first collection, _The Good Thief_ (1988), was made philosophical and reflective with the incorporation of Biblical and mythical allusions. Margaret Atwood, who chose this book for the National Poetry Series, praised Howe’s “poems of obsession that transcend their own dark roots.”[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-:0-2) Additionally, Stanley Kunitz noted, “Her long, deep-breathing lines address the mysteries of flesh and spirit, in terms accessible only to a woman who is very much of our time and yet still in touch with the sacred.” Such an esteemed review justified the selection of _The Good Thief_ for the Lavan Younger Poets Prize from the American Academy of Poets.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-19)

A year after the publication of her first poetry book (1989), Howe’s brother John died from [AIDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIDS "AIDS"). According to Howe in an [AGNI](https://agnionline.bu.edu/about/our-people/authors/marie-howe) interview, “John’s living and dying changed my aesthetic completely.”[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-:0-2) Consequently in 1997, she published a second collection, _What the Living Do_, as an elegy for John which reflected a new style. Stripped of metaphors, her writing was described as “a transparent, accessible documentary of loss” by the [Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/marie-howe).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-:0-2)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-:1-18)

In 2008, Howe distanced herself from the personal narrative and returned to the spiritual style in _The Kingdom of Ordinary Time_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-:0-2) This is most representative of Howe’s style now, a balance between the ordinary and unordinary. It is best put by playwright Eve Ensler, who describes her poems as “a guide to living on the brink of the mystical and the mundane.”[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Howe#cite_note-:1-18)
