The **University of Windsor** (**UWindsor**, **U of W**, or **UWin**) is a [public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_university "Public university")[research university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university "Research university") in [Windsor, Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windsor,_Ontario "Windsor, Ontario"), Canada.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-3) It is Canada's southernmost university.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-aucc.ca-4) It has approximately 17,500 students.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-intldoem-5) The university was incorporated by the provincial government in 1962 and has more than 150,000 alumni.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-6)

The University of Windsor has nine faculties, including the Faculty of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences, the Faculty of Education, the Faculty of Engineering, [Odette School of Business](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odette_School_of_Business "Odette School of Business"), the Faculty of Graduate Studies, the Faculty of Human Kinetics, the [Faculty of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor_Faculty_of_Law "University of Windsor Faculty of Law"), the Faculty of Nursing, and the Faculty of Science. Through its faculties and independent schools, the university has demonstrated its primary research focuses of automotive, environmental, social justice, and international trade research. In recent years, it has increasingly begun focusing on health, natural science, and entrepreneurship research.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-UWindsor_Research-7)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Windsor&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Founding era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Windsor&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Founding era")]

[![Image 7: An aerial photograph of the Assumption College campus in 1928. A few buildings are visible with lots of empty field space.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/Assumption_College_campus_1928.jpg/250px-Assumption_College_campus_1928.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Assumption_College_campus_1928.jpg)

The campus of Assumption College in 1928.

The university dates to the founding of the [Roman Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic "Roman Catholic")[Assumption College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assumption_University_(Windsor,_Ontario) "Assumption University (Windsor, Ontario)") in [Windsor, Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windsor,_Ontario "Windsor, Ontario"), in 1857.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-ce-8) Assumption College, a primarily theological institution, was founded by the [Society of Jesuits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_of_Jesus "Society of Jesus") in 1857. [The Basilian Fathers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregation_of_St._Basil "Congregation of St. Basil") assumed control of the college in 1870. The college grew steadily, expanding its curriculum and affiliating with several other colleges over the years.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-heritagefdn.on.ca-9)

In 1919, Assumption College affiliated with the [University of Western Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Western_Ontario "University of Western Ontario").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-ce-8) This affiliation expanded the curriculum at Assumption, including new general and honours programs for Bachelor of Arts degrees, graduate courses in philosophy, and pre-professional programs in engineering, medicine, and law.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-10)

The school became co-educational in 1934 when it formed and admitted women to attend Holy Names College.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-11) In 1937, the first class of women graduated from Assumption College, receiving Bachelor of Arts degrees.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-12)

Escalating costs forced Assumption College, a Roman Catholic university, to become a public institution to qualify for public support.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-ce-8) In 1953, through an Act of the Ontario Legislature, Assumption College received its own university powers, and ended its affiliation with the University of Western Ontario.

In 1956, the institution's name was changed to Assumption University of Windsor, by an Act of the Ontario Legislature, with Reverend [Eugene Carlisle LeBel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene_Carlisle_LeBel "Eugene Carlisle LeBel"), C.S.B. named as its first President. The recently created Essex College, an independent non-denominational college led by [Frank A. DeMarco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_A._DeMarco "Frank A. DeMarco"), became an affiliate, with responsibility for the Faculty of Applied Science; the Schools of Business Administration and Nursing; and the departments of Biology, Chemistry, Geology and Geography, and Mathematics and Physics.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-AU-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-14)

### Mid-twentieth century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Windsor&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mid-twentieth century")]

In the early 1960s, the city of Windsor's growth and demands for higher education led to further restructuring. A petition was made to the province of Ontario for the creation of a non-denominational University of Windsor by the board of governors and regents of Assumption University and the board of directors of Essex College.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-AU-13) The University of Windsor was established as an institution by the _University of Windsor Act_ on December 19, 1962.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-:1-15) The transition from an historic Roman Catholic university to a non-denominational provincial university was an unprecedented development.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-AU-13)

On July 1, 1963, the entire campus with all of its facilities and faculty became known as the University of Windsor. As a 'federated member', Assumption University remained as an integrated institution, granting degrees only in its Faculty of Theology.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-AU-13) Father Eugene Carlisle LeBel from Assumption became the inaugural president of the University of Windsor, and Frank A. DeMarco, who had been holding both positions of Principal, as well as Dean of Applied Science at Essex College, became the inaugural Vice President. The university's coats of arms were designed by [heraldic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heraldry "Heraldry") expert [Alan Beddoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Beddoe "Alan Beddoe").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-16)

Six months later, Assumption University of Windsor made affiliation agreements with Holy Redeemer College (now [Académie Sainte-Cécile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acad%C3%A9mie_Ste._C%C3%A9cile_International_School "Académie Ste. Cécile International School")), [Canterbury College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_College_(Windsor,_Ontario) "Canterbury College (Windsor, Ontario)") and the new [Iona College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iona_College_(Windsor,_Ontario) "Iona College (Windsor, Ontario)") (affiliated with the [United Church of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Church_of_Canada "United Church of Canada")). Canterbury College became the first [Anglican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Church_of_Canada "Anglican Church of Canada") college in the world to affiliate with a Roman Catholic University.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-AU-13)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-17)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/07/ChryslerBldgUniversity_of_Windsor.jpg/250px-ChryslerBldgUniversity_of_Windsor.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ChryslerBldgUniversity_of_Windsor.jpg)

Lambton Tower on campus.

In 1964, when President LeBel retired, [John Francis Leddy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Francis_Leddy "John Francis Leddy") was appointed president of the University of Windsor, and presided over a period of significant growth.

President Leddy, "concerned that the University of Windsor should emerge as soon as possible from the status and reputation of a College to that of a University", set out to review the existing departments. Based on the strengths in the social sciences, economics, political science and psychology, Leddy proposed to the university's board of governors that a law school be established. In September 1968, the Faculty of Law opened with its first class of students.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-18)

From 1967 to 1977, Windsor grew from approximately 1,500 to 8,000 full-time students.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In the 1980s and early 1990s, this growth continued. Among the new buildings erected were the Odette Business Building and the CAW Student Centre.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The university partnered with [Chrysler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrysler "Chrysler") in 1996 to establish the Automotive Research and Development Centre, a research lab that focuses on automotive research and education.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-19)

### Twenty-first century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Windsor&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Twenty-first century")]

Enrolment reached record heights in 2003 with 16,000 students registered, a 15% increase from the year previous. The increase was driven primarily by first-year students due to the elimination of [Grade 13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario_Academic_Credit "Ontario Academic Credit") in Ontario that year.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-20) The university developed a number of partnerships with businesses and industry, such as a partnership in 2013 with [Maple Leaf Sports and Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maple_Leaf_Sports_and_Entertainment "Maple Leaf Sports and Entertainment") that introduced internships for students and research opportunities.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-21)

In 2008, a satellite campus of the [Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schulich_School_of_Medicine_&_Dentistry "Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry") opened at the University of Windsor.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-22) The partnership between the University of Windsor and the University of Western Ontario followed several years of community and political organizing, and built upon an existing partnership that started in 2002 that sent Western medical students to Windsor for clinical training.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-23) The satellite school initially trained undergraduate medical students in the [Doctor of Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Medicine "Doctor of Medicine") program and has since expanded to offer post-graduate residency programs in family medicine and psychiatry. As of 2023, the program has added almost 100 physicians to the region.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-24)

## Campus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Windsor&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Campus")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Detroit_from_Windsor.JPG/250px-Detroit_from_Windsor.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Detroit_from_Windsor.JPG)

View of the Detroit skyline from the park bordering campus.

Located in Canada's traditional "automotive capital" across the border from [Detroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit "Detroit"), the campus is near the United States and its busy port of entry to and from the United States. It is framed by the [Ambassador Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambassador_Bridge "Ambassador Bridge") to the west and the [Detroit River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit_River "Detroit River") to the north.

The campus covers 51 hectares (130 acres) (contiguous) and is surrounded by a residential neighborhood. The campus features a small [arboretum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arboretum "Arboretum"), which represents most of the species from the [Carolinian forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolinian_forest "Carolinian forest"). Campus is approximately a 10-minute drive from downtown Windsor. The university has moved some academic programs to the downtown core, including Social Work, the Executive and Professional Education program, Music and Fine Arts. Due to its historical roots in multiple religious institutions, the university's campus has many examples of Christian architecture in addition to its modern flagship buildings like the $10-million dollar Joyce Entrepreneurship Centre.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-:0-25)

The War Memorial Hall (more generally known as Memorial Hall) is a landmark building used as classrooms, labs, and offices. Memorial Hall honours alumni who had enlisted and died in the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_World_War "First World War"), and in the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"). A bronze tablet remembers the alumni of Assumption College who died in the Second World War.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-26)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/ba/Dillon_Hall%2C_University_of_Windsor%2C_Windsor%2C_Ontario%2C_2026-04-26_08.jpg/250px-Dillon_Hall%2C_University_of_Windsor%2C_Windsor%2C_Ontario%2C_2026-04-26_08.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dillon_Hall,_University_of_Windsor,_Windsor,_Ontario,_2026-04-26_08.jpg)

Dillon Hall

The Joyce Entrepreneurship Centre (formerly the “Innovation Centre”) is located on the main campus, on the south side of Wyandotte street.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-:0-25) This building houses the EPICentre, and [WEtech Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WEtech_Alliance "WEtech Alliance"). The EPICentre (Entrepreneurship, Practice, and Innovation Centre) is a University of Windsor organization focused on providing students and alumni with the expertise and resources necessary to pursue entrepreneurial goals. The EPICentre is part of the Ontario Centres of Excellence and provides education, mentorship, office space and varying levels of funding to help support startup business.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-27)[WEtech Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WEtech_Alliance "WEtech Alliance") is a similar organization, also being an Ontario Centre of Excellence, whose main focus is to support technology startup companies. They provide services to technology startups in the [Windsor-Essex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essex_County,_Ontario "Essex County, Ontario") and [Chatham-Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chatham-Kent "Chatham-Kent") regions, not exclusively to students and alumni from the University of Windsor.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-28)

The CAW Student Centre is the main, comprehensive centre servicing all student needs. It houses a large food court and the main campus bookstore. Also within the CAW Centre: Student Health Services, a dental office, counselling services, a photographer, a pharmacy, the University of Windsor Students' Alliance (UWSA), a Multi-Faith Space, the campus community radio station [CJAM-FM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CJAM-FM "CJAM-FM"), and an information desk. A large public area beside the food court is available for clubs and informational booths to be set up on certain days. For example, during October there is a period where many Canadian law schools set up booths with representatives who answer questions and provide information to undergraduate students.

The St. Denis Centre, at the south end of campus on College Avenue, is the major athletic and recreational facility for students. It has a weight room, exercise facilities, and a swimming pool. The South Campus Stadium built for the 2005 [Pan American Junior Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan_American_Games "Pan American Games") is beside the St. Denis Centre - which also has dressing rooms for Lancer teams - and borders Huron Church Road, the major avenue to and from the border crossing.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-29) The athletics department has become well known for Track & Field, and Men and Women's Basketball.[_[by whom?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Words\_to\_watch#Unsupported\_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_]

In February 2018, the university announced plans to build a new athletic centre, titled the Lancer Sport and Recreation Centre. The new facility will cost $73 million and be 130,000-square-feet. Unlike the current St. Denis Centre, there will be many separate sections of the facility to host different athletic resources; such as a new gymnasium, pool, fitness gym and many multi-purpose rooms, as opposed to a single general-purpose space.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-30) Construction for the facility began in October, 2018.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-31)

In June 2019, a new research facility opened up on the campus. The new facility, called the Essex Centre of Research (or CORe) is built on to the south side of the existing Essex Hall science facility. It is an open concept 46,000-square-feet facility, featuring state-of-the-art labs and will primarily be used as a research facility.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-32)

### Student residences

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Windsor&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Student residences")]

## Organization and administration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Windsor&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Organization and administration")]

### Governance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Windsor&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Governance")]

The university is governed as a [public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_university "Public university"), [non-profit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonprofit_organization "Nonprofit organization"), and [non-denominational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-denominational "Non-denominational") institution by the _University of Windsor Act, 1962_, which sets out the basic legal obligations and purposes of the institution. Similar to most Canadian universities, the Act establishes the university as a [bicameral institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shared_governance "Shared governance"), governed by a Board of Governors and Senate, and led by a chancellor and president.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-:1-15)

The Board is responsible for the oversight of all operational aspects of the university, including strategic direction, budgets, property management, and accountability for the university's financial, human, and physical resources.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-35) The Board is also responsible for appointing the chancellor, and the president and vice-chancellor. There are 32 members of the board, 20 external and 12 internal; this size was considered to be large without a compelling reason by the [Auditor General of Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auditor_General_of_Ontario "Auditor General of Ontario") in a 2022 audit of Ontario universities.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-:2-36)

The [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_senate "Academic senate") is the supreme governing body of the university in academic matters. It is responsible for establishing academic policy, approving new programs and curricular changes, setting admission requirements, and overseeing academic regulation and discipline. It is the Senate that grants degrees, and has the authority to revoke them. The Senate is constituted by members of the [faculty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_staff "Academic staff"), who are either appointed ex-officio by virtue of their role, or elected by the faculty members from their home constituencies. Several students, staff members, and an alumni representative are also appointed to the Senate.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-:1-15) There are several standing committees of the Senate that oversee different aspects of the Senate's mandate.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-37)

As is common in Canada, Windsor is formally headed by the [chancellor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor_(education) "Chancellor (education)") and led on a day-to-day basis by the [president and vice-chancellor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor_(education)#Vice-chancellor "Chancellor (education)"). The chancellor is the titular head of the university and confers all degrees. The role is mainly ceremonial. Since May 2019 this has been [Mary Jo Haddad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Jo_Haddad "Mary Jo Haddad"), a Windsor nursing alumnus and the first woman to take this role, who succeeded [Ed Lumley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Lumley "Ed Lumley").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-38)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-39) The president serves as the [chief executive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_executive_officer "Chief executive officer") of the university and the chair of the Senate. As per the Act, the president has supervision and direction over the academic work and administration of the university. The current president is Robert Gordon who has been in this role since September 2019.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-40)

### Finances

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Windsor&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Finances")]

Windsor has an endowment of $139 million as of April 2023. The university's total assets (including its campus) are valued at $877 million.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-44) Its operating budget for the 2023-2024 academic year was $345 million. The [Government of Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Ontario "Government of Ontario") provided 29% of the university's operating revenue, while tuition fees accounted for the bulk of the remainder at 69%. International student tuition fees comprised 62% of all tuition fee revenue.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-45)

The growing reliance on tuition fees from international students is not unique to the University of Windsor and is common at Ontario's public universities.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-:2-36) A 2023 [blue-ribbon panel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue-ribbon_committee "Blue-ribbon committee") of experts reviewed the financial sustainability of Ontario's universities and colleges and found that Ontario funds universities at just 57% of the national average, due to the government's policies that reduced direct funding to institutions and cut tuition fees for domestic students.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-46)

## Academics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Windsor&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Academics")]

The University of Windsor is a public research university and a member of [Universities Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universities_Canada "Universities Canada").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-47) Full-time undergraduate students comprise the majority of the university's enrolment, with the university offering over than 120 majors and minors. There are more than 70 master's (course and research based) and doctoral degree programs.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-intldoem-5)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-48) In 2020, the university conferred more than 2,700 bachelor's degrees, 1,900 master's degrees, and 50 doctoral degrees.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-49)

The University of Windsor's philosophy department is known for its work in [informal logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Informal_logic "Informal logic"), and regularly hosts an international argumentation conference through the Ontario Society for the Study of Argumentation.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-50) Students, faculty, and visiting researchers collaborate in the inter-departmental research group the [Centre for Research in Reasoning, Argumentation, and Rhetoric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_for_Research_in_Reasoning,_Argumentation,_and_Rhetoric "Centre for Research in Reasoning, Argumentation, and Rhetoric").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-51) As of 2016, the University of Windsor offers an interdisciplinary PhD in Argumentation Studies, the only graduate program in North America with a focus on this field.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-52)

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0d/OdetteBldg_University_of_Windsor.jpg/250px-OdetteBldg_University_of_Windsor.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:OdetteBldg_University_of_Windsor.jpg)

Faculty of Business, Odette Building.

The Faculty of Nursing offers several undergraduate and graduate programs. This includes the accredited clinical [Bachelor of Science in Nursing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science_in_Nursing "Bachelor of Science in Nursing") and [nurse practitioner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nurse_practitioner "Nurse practitioner") programs, along with a research-based doctoral program.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-53)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-54) The undergraduate program is also offered in collaboration with [St. Clair College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Clair_College "St. Clair College").

The [Faculty of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor_Faculty_of_Law "University of Windsor Faculty of Law"), one of seven in Ontario, has a major teaching and research focus on social justice issues and criminal law. Two [legal clinics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legal_clinic "Legal clinic") offer training experience for students. The faculty offers a dual undergraduate law program with the [University of Detroit Mercy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Detroit_Mercy "University of Detroit Mercy"), training students in both Canadian and US law, one of the only programs of this kind in North America.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-55)

University of Windsor also provides Inter-Faculty Programs offering cross-departmental majors like [Forensics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forensic_science "Forensic science"), [Environmental studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_studies "Environmental studies") and Arts & Science concentration. There are nine [cooperative education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooperative_education "Cooperative education") programs for 1,100 students.

### Scholarships

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Windsor&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Scholarships")]

One of the largest scholarship programs at the institution is the [Outstanding Scholars](https://www.uwindsor.ca/outstandingscholars/) program. It is unique for its interdisciplinary breadth, experiential learning depth an proportionate scale. Secondary students can apply to get a scholarship, mentorship, and leadership curriculum. After students complete their first year, the highest achieving students in each undergraduate faculty are invigted to compete for one of approximately 85 spots in the full Outstanding Scholars program. Full Outstanding Scholars are funded for six paid placements between their second and fourth year of study. What makes the program unique is its scale and the fact that students can become research assistants across any faculty on campus. Students also become part of the [UWill Discover ecosystem](https://www.uwindsor.ca/uwilldiscover/) which includes a [journal](https://www.uwindsor.ca/uwilldiscover/314/uwill-discover-journal), [podcast](https://www.uwindsor.ca/uwilldiscover/317/uwill-discover-podcast) and [annual conference](https://www.uwindsor.ca/uwilldiscover/).

The university joined Project Hero, a scholarship program cofounded by General (Ret'd) [Rick Hillier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Hillier "Rick Hillier"), for the families of fallen [Canadian Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Forces "Canadian Forces") members.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-60)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-61)

The university established Rosa Schreiber Award with the assistance of former University of Windsor Professor Economics, [Alan A. Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_A._Brown "Alan A. Brown"). From the university's Senate Committee on Student Awards: The competition award is open to arts or social science students in Year 2 or beyond. Applicants must submit a 1,500–2,000-word essay on some aspect of moral courage. Submission must be made to the Office of Student Awards. This competition will be held in alternate years. It was established in 1995 to honour Rosa Schreiber, an Austrian freedom fighter who risked her life to help others during World War II.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The **University of Windsor** (**UWindsor**, **U of W**, or **UWin**) is a [public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_university "Public university")[research university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university "Research university") in [Windsor, Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windsor,_Ontario "Windsor, Ontario"), Canada.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-3) It is Canada's southernmost university.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-aucc.ca-4) It has approximately 17,500 students.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-intldoem-5) The university was incorporated by the provincial government in 1962 and has more than 150,000 alumni.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-6)

The University of Windsor has nine faculties, including the Faculty of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences, the Faculty of Education, the Faculty of Engineering, [Odette School of Business](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odette_School_of_Business "Odette School of Business"), the Faculty of Graduate Studies, the Faculty of Human Kinetics, the [Faculty of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor_Faculty_of_Law "University of Windsor Faculty of Law"), the Faculty of Nursing, and the Faculty of Science. Through its faculties and independent schools, the university has demonstrated its primary research focuses of automotive, environmental, social justice, and international trade research. In recent years, it has increasingly begun focusing on health, natural science, and entrepreneurship research.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-UWindsor_Research-7)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Windsor&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Founding era

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Windsor&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Founding era")]

[![Image 7: An aerial photograph of the Assumption College campus in 1928. A few buildings are visible with lots of empty field space.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/Assumption_College_campus_1928.jpg/250px-Assumption_College_campus_1928.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Assumption_College_campus_1928.jpg)

The campus of Assumption College in 1928.

The university dates to the founding of the [Roman Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic "Roman Catholic")[Assumption College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assumption_University_(Windsor,_Ontario) "Assumption University (Windsor, Ontario)") in [Windsor, Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windsor,_Ontario "Windsor, Ontario"), in 1857.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-ce-8) Assumption College, a primarily theological institution, was founded by the [Society of Jesuits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_of_Jesus "Society of Jesus") in 1857. [The Basilian Fathers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregation_of_St._Basil "Congregation of St. Basil") assumed control of the college in 1870. The college grew steadily, expanding its curriculum and affiliating with several other colleges over the years.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-heritagefdn.on.ca-9)

In 1919, Assumption College affiliated with the [University of Western Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Western_Ontario "University of Western Ontario").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-ce-8) This affiliation expanded the curriculum at Assumption, including new general and honours programs for Bachelor of Arts degrees, graduate courses in philosophy, and pre-professional programs in engineering, medicine, and law.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-10)

The school became co-educational in 1934 when it formed and admitted women to attend Holy Names College.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-11) In 1937, the first class of women graduated from Assumption College, receiving Bachelor of Arts degrees.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-12)

Escalating costs forced Assumption College, a Roman Catholic university, to become a public institution to qualify for public support.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-ce-8) In 1953, through an Act of the Ontario Legislature, Assumption College received its own university powers, and ended its affiliation with the University of Western Ontario.

In 1956, the institution's name was changed to Assumption University of Windsor, by an Act of the Ontario Legislature, with Reverend [Eugene Carlisle LeBel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene_Carlisle_LeBel "Eugene Carlisle LeBel"), C.S.B. named as its first President. The recently created Essex College, an independent non-denominational college led by [Frank A. DeMarco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_A._DeMarco "Frank A. DeMarco"), became an affiliate, with responsibility for the Faculty of Applied Science; the Schools of Business Administration and Nursing; and the departments of Biology, Chemistry, Geology and Geography, and Mathematics and Physics.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-AU-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-14)

### Mid-twentieth century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Windsor&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mid-twentieth century")]

In the early 1960s, the city of Windsor's growth and demands for higher education led to further restructuring. A petition was made to the province of Ontario for the creation of a non-denominational University of Windsor by the board of governors and regents of Assumption University and the board of directors of Essex College.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-AU-13) The University of Windsor was established as an institution by the _University of Windsor Act_ on December 19, 1962.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-:1-15) The transition from an historic Roman Catholic university to a non-denominational provincial university was an unprecedented development.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-AU-13)

On July 1, 1963, the entire campus with all of its facilities and faculty became known as the University of Windsor. As a 'federated member', Assumption University remained as an integrated institution, granting degrees only in its Faculty of Theology.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-AU-13) Father Eugene Carlisle LeBel from Assumption became the inaugural president of the University of Windsor, and Frank A. DeMarco, who had been holding both positions of Principal, as well as Dean of Applied Science at Essex College, became the inaugural Vice President. The university's coats of arms were designed by [heraldic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heraldry "Heraldry") expert [Alan Beddoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Beddoe "Alan Beddoe").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-16)

Six months later, Assumption University of Windsor made affiliation agreements with Holy Redeemer College (now [Académie Sainte-Cécile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acad%C3%A9mie_Ste._C%C3%A9cile_International_School "Académie Ste. Cécile International School")), [Canterbury College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_College_(Windsor,_Ontario) "Canterbury College (Windsor, Ontario)") and the new [Iona College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iona_College_(Windsor,_Ontario) "Iona College (Windsor, Ontario)") (affiliated with the [United Church of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Church_of_Canada "United Church of Canada")). Canterbury College became the first [Anglican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Church_of_Canada "Anglican Church of Canada") college in the world to affiliate with a Roman Catholic University.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-AU-13)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-17)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/07/ChryslerBldgUniversity_of_Windsor.jpg/250px-ChryslerBldgUniversity_of_Windsor.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:ChryslerBldgUniversity_of_Windsor.jpg)

Lambton Tower on campus.

In 1964, when President LeBel retired, [John Francis Leddy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Francis_Leddy "John Francis Leddy") was appointed president of the University of Windsor, and presided over a period of significant growth.

President Leddy, "concerned that the University of Windsor should emerge as soon as possible from the status and reputation of a College to that of a University", set out to review the existing departments. Based on the strengths in the social sciences, economics, political science and psychology, Leddy proposed to the university's board of governors that a law school be established. In September 1968, the Faculty of Law opened with its first class of students.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-18)

From 1967 to 1977, Windsor grew from approximately 1,500 to 8,000 full-time students.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In the 1980s and early 1990s, this growth continued. Among the new buildings erected were the Odette Business Building and the CAW Student Centre.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The university partnered with [Chrysler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chrysler "Chrysler") in 1996 to establish the Automotive Research and Development Centre, a research lab that focuses on automotive research and education.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-19)

### Twenty-first century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Windsor&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Twenty-first century")]

Enrolment reached record heights in 2003 with 16,000 students registered, a 15% increase from the year previous. The increase was driven primarily by first-year students due to the elimination of [Grade 13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario_Academic_Credit "Ontario Academic Credit") in Ontario that year.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-20) The university developed a number of partnerships with businesses and industry, such as a partnership in 2013 with [Maple Leaf Sports and Entertainment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maple_Leaf_Sports_and_Entertainment "Maple Leaf Sports and Entertainment") that introduced internships for students and research opportunities.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-21)

In 2008, a satellite campus of the [Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schulich_School_of_Medicine_&_Dentistry "Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry") opened at the University of Windsor.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-22) The partnership between the University of Windsor and the University of Western Ontario followed several years of community and political organizing, and built upon an existing partnership that started in 2002 that sent Western medical students to Windsor for clinical training.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-23) The satellite school initially trained undergraduate medical students in the [Doctor of Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Medicine "Doctor of Medicine") program and has since expanded to offer post-graduate residency programs in family medicine and psychiatry. As of 2023, the program has added almost 100 physicians to the region.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-24)

## Campus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Windsor&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Campus")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Detroit_from_Windsor.JPG/250px-Detroit_from_Windsor.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Detroit_from_Windsor.JPG)

View of the Detroit skyline from the park bordering campus.

Located in Canada's traditional "automotive capital" across the border from [Detroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit "Detroit"), the campus is near the United States and its busy port of entry to and from the United States. It is framed by the [Ambassador Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambassador_Bridge "Ambassador Bridge") to the west and the [Detroit River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit_River "Detroit River") to the north.

The campus covers 51 hectares (130 acres) (contiguous) and is surrounded by a residential neighborhood. The campus features a small [arboretum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arboretum "Arboretum"), which represents most of the species from the [Carolinian forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolinian_forest "Carolinian forest"). Campus is approximately a 10-minute drive from downtown Windsor. The university has moved some academic programs to the downtown core, including Social Work, the Executive and Professional Education program, Music and Fine Arts. Due to its historical roots in multiple religious institutions, the university's campus has many examples of Christian architecture in addition to its modern flagship buildings like the $10-million dollar Joyce Entrepreneurship Centre.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-:0-25)

The War Memorial Hall (more generally known as Memorial Hall) is a landmark building used as classrooms, labs, and offices. Memorial Hall honours alumni who had enlisted and died in the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_World_War "First World War"), and in the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"). A bronze tablet remembers the alumni of Assumption College who died in the Second World War.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-26)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/ba/Dillon_Hall%2C_University_of_Windsor%2C_Windsor%2C_Ontario%2C_2026-04-26_08.jpg/250px-Dillon_Hall%2C_University_of_Windsor%2C_Windsor%2C_Ontario%2C_2026-04-26_08.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dillon_Hall,_University_of_Windsor,_Windsor,_Ontario,_2026-04-26_08.jpg)

Dillon Hall

The Joyce Entrepreneurship Centre (formerly the “Innovation Centre”) is located on the main campus, on the south side of Wyandotte street.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-:0-25) This building houses the EPICentre, and [WEtech Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WEtech_Alliance "WEtech Alliance"). The EPICentre (Entrepreneurship, Practice, and Innovation Centre) is a University of Windsor organization focused on providing students and alumni with the expertise and resources necessary to pursue entrepreneurial goals. The EPICentre is part of the Ontario Centres of Excellence and provides education, mentorship, office space and varying levels of funding to help support startup business.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-27)[WEtech Alliance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WEtech_Alliance "WEtech Alliance") is a similar organization, also being an Ontario Centre of Excellence, whose main focus is to support technology startup companies. They provide services to technology startups in the [Windsor-Essex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essex_County,_Ontario "Essex County, Ontario") and [Chatham-Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chatham-Kent "Chatham-Kent") regions, not exclusively to students and alumni from the University of Windsor.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-28)

The CAW Student Centre is the main, comprehensive centre servicing all student needs. It houses a large food court and the main campus bookstore. Also within the CAW Centre: Student Health Services, a dental office, counselling services, a photographer, a pharmacy, the University of Windsor Students' Alliance (UWSA), a Multi-Faith Space, the campus community radio station [CJAM-FM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CJAM-FM "CJAM-FM"), and an information desk. A large public area beside the food court is available for clubs and informational booths to be set up on certain days. For example, during October there is a period where many Canadian law schools set up booths with representatives who answer questions and provide information to undergraduate students.

The St. Denis Centre, at the south end of campus on College Avenue, is the major athletic and recreational facility for students. It has a weight room, exercise facilities, and a swimming pool. The South Campus Stadium built for the 2005 [Pan American Junior Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan_American_Games "Pan American Games") is beside the St. Denis Centre - which also has dressing rooms for Lancer teams - and borders Huron Church Road, the major avenue to and from the border crossing.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-29) The athletics department has become well known for Track & Field, and Men and Women's Basketball.[_[by whom?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Words\_to\_watch#Unsupported\_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_]

In February 2018, the university announced plans to build a new athletic centre, titled the Lancer Sport and Recreation Centre. The new facility will cost $73 million and be 130,000-square-feet. Unlike the current St. Denis Centre, there will be many separate sections of the facility to host different athletic resources; such as a new gymnasium, pool, fitness gym and many multi-purpose rooms, as opposed to a single general-purpose space.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-30) Construction for the facility began in October, 2018.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-31)

In June 2019, a new research facility opened up on the campus. The new facility, called the Essex Centre of Research (or CORe) is built on to the south side of the existing Essex Hall science facility. It is an open concept 46,000-square-feet facility, featuring state-of-the-art labs and will primarily be used as a research facility.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-32)

## Organization and administration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Windsor&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Organization and administration")]

### Governance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Windsor&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Governance")]

The university is governed as a [public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_university "Public university"), [non-profit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nonprofit_organization "Nonprofit organization"), and [non-denominational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-denominational "Non-denominational") institution by the _University of Windsor Act, 1962_, which sets out the basic legal obligations and purposes of the institution. Similar to most Canadian universities, the Act establishes the university as a [bicameral institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shared_governance "Shared governance"), governed by a Board of Governors and Senate, and led by a chancellor and president.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-:1-15)

The Board is responsible for the oversight of all operational aspects of the university, including strategic direction, budgets, property management, and accountability for the university's financial, human, and physical resources.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-35) The Board is also responsible for appointing the chancellor, and the president and vice-chancellor. There are 32 members of the board, 20 external and 12 internal; this size was considered to be large without a compelling reason by the [Auditor General of Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auditor_General_of_Ontario "Auditor General of Ontario") in a 2022 audit of Ontario universities.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-:2-36)

The [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_senate "Academic senate") is the supreme governing body of the university in academic matters. It is responsible for establishing academic policy, approving new programs and curricular changes, setting admission requirements, and overseeing academic regulation and discipline. It is the Senate that grants degrees, and has the authority to revoke them. The Senate is constituted by members of the [faculty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_staff "Academic staff"), who are either appointed ex-officio by virtue of their role, or elected by the faculty members from their home constituencies. Several students, staff members, and an alumni representative are also appointed to the Senate.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-:1-15) There are several standing committees of the Senate that oversee different aspects of the Senate's mandate.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-37)

As is common in Canada, Windsor is formally headed by the [chancellor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor_(education) "Chancellor (education)") and led on a day-to-day basis by the [president and vice-chancellor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor_(education)#Vice-chancellor "Chancellor (education)"). The chancellor is the titular head of the university and confers all degrees. The role is mainly ceremonial. Since May 2019 this has been [Mary Jo Haddad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Jo_Haddad "Mary Jo Haddad"), a Windsor nursing alumnus and the first woman to take this role, who succeeded [Ed Lumley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Lumley "Ed Lumley").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-38)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-39) The president serves as the [chief executive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_executive_officer "Chief executive officer") of the university and the chair of the Senate. As per the Act, the president has supervision and direction over the academic work and administration of the university. The current president is Robert Gordon who has been in this role since September 2019.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-40)

### Federated and affiliated institutions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Windsor&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Federated and affiliated institutions")]

The University of Windsor has three [federated or affiliated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affiliated_school "Affiliated school") institutions. It is federated with [Assumption University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assumption_University_(Windsor,_Ontario) "Assumption University (Windsor, Ontario)"), a [Roman Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church") university offering graduate degree programs in religious subjects. The university is affiliated with [Canterbury College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury_College_(Windsor,_Ontario) "Canterbury College (Windsor, Ontario)"), a public liberal arts college affiliated with the [Anglican Church of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglican_Church_of_Canada "Anglican Church of Canada"), and [Iona College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iona_College_(Windsor,_Ontario) "Iona College (Windsor, Ontario)"), a public liberal arts college formerly affiliated with the [United Church of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Church_of_Canada "United Church of Canada").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-43)

### Finances

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Windsor&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Finances")]

Windsor has an endowment of $139 million as of April 2023. The university's total assets (including its campus) are valued at $877 million.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-44) Its operating budget for the 2023-2024 academic year was $345 million. The [Government of Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Ontario "Government of Ontario") provided 29% of the university's operating revenue, while tuition fees accounted for the bulk of the remainder at 69%. International student tuition fees comprised 62% of all tuition fee revenue.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-45)

The growing reliance on tuition fees from international students is not unique to the University of Windsor and is common at Ontario's public universities.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-:2-36) A 2023 [blue-ribbon panel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue-ribbon_committee "Blue-ribbon committee") of experts reviewed the financial sustainability of Ontario's universities and colleges and found that Ontario funds universities at just 57% of the national average, due to the government's policies that reduced direct funding to institutions and cut tuition fees for domestic students.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-46)

## Academics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Windsor&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Academics")]

The University of Windsor is a public research university and a member of [Universities Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universities_Canada "Universities Canada").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-47) Full-time undergraduate students comprise the majority of the university's enrolment, with the university offering over than 120 majors and minors. There are more than 70 master's (course and research based) and doctoral degree programs.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-intldoem-5)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-48) In 2020, the university conferred more than 2,700 bachelor's degrees, 1,900 master's degrees, and 50 doctoral degrees.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-49)

The University of Windsor's philosophy department is known for its work in [informal logic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Informal_logic "Informal logic"), and regularly hosts an international argumentation conference through the Ontario Society for the Study of Argumentation.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-50) Students, faculty, and visiting researchers collaborate in the inter-departmental research group the [Centre for Research in Reasoning, Argumentation, and Rhetoric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_for_Research_in_Reasoning,_Argumentation,_and_Rhetoric "Centre for Research in Reasoning, Argumentation, and Rhetoric").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-51) As of 2016, the University of Windsor offers an interdisciplinary PhD in Argumentation Studies, the only graduate program in North America with a focus on this field.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-52)

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0d/OdetteBldg_University_of_Windsor.jpg/250px-OdetteBldg_University_of_Windsor.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:OdetteBldg_University_of_Windsor.jpg)

Faculty of Business, Odette Building.

The Faculty of Nursing offers several undergraduate and graduate programs. This includes the accredited clinical [Bachelor of Science in Nursing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science_in_Nursing "Bachelor of Science in Nursing") and [nurse practitioner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nurse_practitioner "Nurse practitioner") programs, along with a research-based doctoral program.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-53)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-54) The undergraduate program is also offered in collaboration with [St. Clair College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Clair_College "St. Clair College").

The [Faculty of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor_Faculty_of_Law "University of Windsor Faculty of Law"), one of seven in Ontario, has a major teaching and research focus on social justice issues and criminal law. Two [legal clinics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legal_clinic "Legal clinic") offer training experience for students. The faculty offers a dual undergraduate law program with the [University of Detroit Mercy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Detroit_Mercy "University of Detroit Mercy"), training students in both Canadian and US law, one of the only programs of this kind in North America.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-55)

University of Windsor also provides Inter-Faculty Programs offering cross-departmental majors like [Forensics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forensic_science "Forensic science"), [Environmental studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_studies "Environmental studies") and Arts & Science concentration. There are nine [cooperative education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooperative_education "Cooperative education") programs for 1,100 students.

### Scholarships

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Windsor&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Scholarships")]

One of the largest scholarship programs at the institution is the [Outstanding Scholars](https://www.uwindsor.ca/outstandingscholars/) program. It is unique for its interdisciplinary breadth, experiential learning depth an proportionate scale. Secondary students can apply to get a scholarship, mentorship, and leadership curriculum. After students complete their first year, the highest achieving students in each undergraduate faculty are invigted to compete for one of approximately 85 spots in the full Outstanding Scholars program. Full Outstanding Scholars are funded for six paid placements between their second and fourth year of study. What makes the program unique is its scale and the fact that students can become research assistants across any faculty on campus. Students also become part of the [UWill Discover ecosystem](https://www.uwindsor.ca/uwilldiscover/) which includes a [journal](https://www.uwindsor.ca/uwilldiscover/314/uwill-discover-journal), [podcast](https://www.uwindsor.ca/uwilldiscover/317/uwill-discover-podcast) and [annual conference](https://www.uwindsor.ca/uwilldiscover/).

The university joined Project Hero, a scholarship program cofounded by General (Ret'd) [Rick Hillier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Hillier "Rick Hillier"), for the families of fallen [Canadian Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Forces "Canadian Forces") members.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-60)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-61)

The university established Rosa Schreiber Award with the assistance of former University of Windsor Professor Economics, [Alan A. Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_A._Brown "Alan A. Brown"). From the university's Senate Committee on Student Awards: The competition award is open to arts or social science students in Year 2 or beyond. Applicants must submit a 1,500–2,000-word essay on some aspect of moral courage. Submission must be made to the Office of Student Awards. This competition will be held in alternate years. It was established in 1995 to honour Rosa Schreiber, an Austrian freedom fighter who risked her life to help others during World War II.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

There are three student unions at Windsor. The University of Windsor Students' Alliance, otherwise known as the UWSA, represents all full-time [undergraduate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undergraduate "Undergraduate") students at the University of Windsor, located in [Windsor, Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windsor,_Ontario "Windsor, Ontario"), Canada. It provides services such as an Office of Student Empowerment, financial awards, a [food pantry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_bank "Food bank"), representation on various University of Windsor bodies, a weekly student newspaper, _The Lance_, and various other services and programs.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-68)

The Organization of Part-time University Students (OPUS) represents part-time undergraduate students, while the Graduate Student Society represents all graduate students at the university.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-69)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-70) All three student unions are affiliated with the [Canadian Federation of Students](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Federation_of_Students "Canadian Federation of Students").[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Windsor#cite_note-71)
