**Dame Carol Ann Duffy** (born 23 December 1955) is a Scottish[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-Forbes-3) poet and playwright. She is a professor of contemporary poetry at [Manchester Metropolitan University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_Metropolitan_University "Manchester Metropolitan University"), and was appointed [Poet Laureate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poet_Laureate_of_the_United_Kingdom "Poet Laureate of the United Kingdom") in May 2009,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-about-4) serving in this position until her term ended in 2019. She was the first female, the first Scottish-born and the first openly lesbian poet to hold the Poet Laureate position.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-5)

Her collections include _Standing Female Nude_ (1985), winner of a [Scottish Arts Council Book Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Mortgage_Investment_Trust_Book_Awards "Scottish Mortgage Investment Trust Book Awards"); _Selling Manhattan_ (1987), which won a [Somerset Maugham Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerset_Maugham_Award "Somerset Maugham Award"); _Mean Time_ (1993), which won the [Whitbread Poetry Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Book_Award_for_Poetry "Costa Book Award for Poetry"); and _[Rapture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapture\_(poetry\_collection) "Rapture (poetry collection)")_ (2005), which won the [T. S. Eliot Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._S._Eliot_Prize "T. S. Eliot Prize"). Her poems address issues such as [oppression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oppression "Oppression"), gender, and violence, in accessible language.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-EB-6)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carol_Ann_Duffy&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Carol Ann Duffy was born into a Roman Catholic family in the [Gorbals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorbals "Gorbals")[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-scottishpoetrylibrary-7) area of [Glasgow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glasgow "Glasgow"). She was the daughter of Mary (née Black) and Frank Duffy, an electrical fitter.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-Forbes-3) Her mother's parents were Irish, and her father had Irish grandparents.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-scottishpoetrylibrary-7) The eldest of five siblings, she has four brothers: Frank, Adrian, Eugene and Tim. The family moved to [Stafford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stafford "Stafford"), England, when Duffy was six years old. Her father worked for [English Electric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Electric "English Electric"). A trade unionist, he stood unsuccessfully as a parliamentary candidate for the [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK) "Labour Party (UK)") in 1983 in addition to managing [Stafford Football Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stafford_Town_F.C. "Stafford Town F.C.").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-Forbes-3)

Duffy was educated in Stafford at Saint Austin's RC Primary School (1962–1967), St. Joseph's Convent School (1967–1970), and [Stafford Girls' High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Edward_VI_High_School,_Stafford "King Edward VI High School, Stafford") (1970–1974), her literary talent encouraged by two English teachers, June Scriven at St Joseph's, and Jim Walker at Stafford Girls' High.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-Forbes-3) She was a passionate reader from an early age, and always wanted to be a writer, producing poems from the age of 11. When one of her English teachers died, she wrote:

> You sat on your desk,  
>  swinging your legs,   
>  reading a poem by Yeats   
>  to the bored girls,   
>  except my heart stumbled and blushed  
>  as it fell in love with the words and I saw the tree   
>  in the scratched old desk under my hands,   
>  heard the bird in the oak outside scribble itself on the air.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-8)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carol_Ann_Duffy&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

> Some days, although we cannot pray, a prayer  
>  utters itself. So, a woman will lift  
>  her head from the sieve of her hands and stare  
>  at the minims sung by a tree, a sudden gift.  
>   
>  Some nights, although we are faithless, the truth  
>  enters our hearts, that small familiar pain;  
>  then a man will stand stock-still, hearing his youth  
>  in the distant Latin chanting of a train.

—From "Prayer",   
_Mean Time_, Anvil, 1994[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-9)

When Duffy was 15, June Scriven sent her poems to _Outposts_, a publisher of pamphlets, where it was read by the bookseller Bernard Stone, who published some of them. When she was 16, she met [Adrian Henri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrian_Henri "Adrian Henri"), 39 at the time, one of the [Liverpool poets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_poets "Liverpool poets"), and decided she wanted to be with him; she then lived with him for 10 years until they split in 1982. "He gave me confidence," she said, "he was great. It was all poetry, very heady, and he was never faithful. He thought poets had a duty to be unfaithful."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-Winterson-10)

She applied to the [University of Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Liverpool "University of Liverpool") to be near him, and began a [philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophy "Philosophy") degree there in 1974. She had two plays performed at the [Liverpool Playhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_Playhouse "Liverpool Playhouse"), wrote a pamphlet, _Fifth Last Song_, and received an honours degree in philosophy in 1977.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-Forbes-3) She won the [National Poetry Competition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Poetry_Competition "National Poetry Competition") in 1983. She worked as poetry critic for _The Guardian_ from 1988 to 1989, and was editor of the poetry magazine, [_Ambit_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambit_(magazine) "Ambit (magazine)"). In 1996, she was appointed as a lecturer in poetry at [Manchester Metropolitan University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_Metropolitan_University "Manchester Metropolitan University"), and later became creative director of its Writing School.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-EB-6)

Duffy was a contender for the post of [Poet Laureate of the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poet_Laureate_of_the_United_Kingdom "Poet Laureate of the United Kingdom") in 1999 after the death of [Ted Hughes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Hughes "Ted Hughes"), but lost out to [Andrew Motion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Motion "Andrew Motion"). Duffy said she would not have accepted the position at that time anyway, because she was in a relationship with Scottish poet [Jackie Kay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Kay "Jackie Kay"), had a young daughter, and would not have welcomed the public attention.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-11) In the same year, she was elected as a Fellow of the [Royal Society of Literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Society_of_Literature "Royal Society of Literature").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-12)

She was appointed as Poet Laureate on 1 May 2009,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-13) when Motion's 10-year term was over. Duffy was featured on _[The South Bank Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_South\_Bank\_Show "The South Bank Show")_ with [Melvyn Bragg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melvyn_Bragg "Melvyn Bragg") in December 2009[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-14) and on 7 December she presented the [Turner Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turner_Prize "Turner Prize") to artist [Richard Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Wright_(artist) "Richard Wright (artist)").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-15)

Duffy received an Honorary Doctorate from [Heriot-Watt University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heriot-Watt_University "Heriot-Watt University") in 2009.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-16)

In 2015, Duffy was elected as an [Honorary Fellow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honorary_Fellow "Honorary Fellow") of the [British Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Academy "British Academy").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-17)

### Poet laureate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carol_Ann_Duffy&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Poet laureate")]

In her first poem as poet laureate, Duffy tackled the scandal over British [MPs' expenses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_Parliamentary_expenses_scandal "United Kingdom Parliamentary expenses scandal") in the format of a [sonnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonnet "Sonnet").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-18) Her second, "[Last Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Post_(poem) "Last Post (poem)")", was commissioned by the BBC to mark the deaths of [Henry Allingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Allingham "Henry Allingham") and [Harry Patch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Patch "Harry Patch"), the last remaining British soldiers to fight in World War I.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-19) Her third, "The Twelve Days of Christmas 2009", addresses current events such as [species extinction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Species_extinction "Species extinction"), the [climate change conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copenhagen_United_Nations_Climate_Change_Conference "Copenhagen United Nations Climate Change Conference") in Copenhagen, the [banking crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banking_crisis "Banking crisis"), and the [war in Afghanistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_in_Afghanistan_(2001%E2%80%93present) "War in Afghanistan (2001–present)").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-20) In March 2010, she wrote "Achilles (for David Beckham)" about the [Achilles tendon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achilles_tendon "Achilles tendon") injury that left [David Beckham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Beckham "David Beckham") out of the English football team at the [2010 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_FIFA_World_Cup "2010 FIFA World Cup");[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-21) the poem was published in _[The Daily Mirror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily\_Mirror "Daily Mirror")_ and treats modern celebrity culture as a kind of mythicisation.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-22) "Silver Lining," written in April 2010, acknowledges the grounding of flights caused by the ash of the Icelandic volcano [Eyjafjallajökull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eyjafjallaj%C3%B6kull "Eyjafjallajökull").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-23) On 30 August 2010 she premièred her poem "Vigil" for the [Manchester Pride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_Pride "Manchester Pride") Candlelight Vigil in memory of [LGBTQ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBTQ "LGBTQ") people who have lost their lives to [HIV/AIDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV/AIDS "HIV/AIDS").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-24)

Duffy wrote a 46-line poem, "Rings," for the 2011 [wedding of Prince William and Catherine Middleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wedding_of_Prince_William_and_Catherine_Middleton "Wedding of Prince William and Catherine Middleton"). The poem celebrates the rings found in nature and does not specifically mention the couple's names. It begins _for both to say_ and continues: "I might have raised your hand to the sky / to give you the ring surrounding the moon / or looked to twin the rings of your eyes / with mine / or added a ring to the rings of a tree / by forming a handheld circle with you, thee, / ...". She wrote the verse with Stephen Raw, a textual artist, and a signed print of the work was sent to the couple as a wedding gift.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-26) Duffy also wrote the poem "The Throne," which she composed for the 60th anniversary of [Queen Elizabeth II's coronation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronation_of_Queen_Elizabeth_II "Coronation of Queen Elizabeth II").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-27)

In _[Stylist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stylist\_(magazine) "Stylist (magazine)")_ magazine,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-Interview-28) Duffy said of becoming poet laureate: "There's no requirement. I do get asked to do things and so far I've been happy to do them." She also spoke about being appointed to the role by [Queen Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II"), saying: "She's lovely! I met her before I became poet laureate but when I was appointed I had an 'audience' with her which meant we were alone, at the palace, for the first time. We chatted about poetry. Her mother was friends with [Ted Hughes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Hughes "Ted Hughes") whose poetry I admire a lot. We spoke about his influence on me."[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-Interview-28)

Duffy stood down as laureate in May 2019.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-Guardian181027-29)

## Poetry

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carol_Ann_Duffy&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Poetry")]

### Style

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carol_Ann_Duffy&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Style")]

Duffy's work explores both everyday experience and the rich fantasy life of herself and others. In dramatizing scenes from childhood, adolescence, and adult life, she discovers moments of consolation through love, memory, and language. [Charlotte Mendelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte_Mendelson "Charlotte Mendelson") writes in _The Observer_:

> Part of Duffy's talent– besides her ear for ordinary eloquence, her gorgeous, powerful, throwaway lines, her subtlety– is her ventriloquism. Like the best of her novelist peers... she slides in and out of her characters' lives on a stream of possessions, aspirations, idioms and turns of phrase. However, she is also a time-traveller and a shape-shifter, gliding from [Troy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troy "Troy") to Hollywood, galaxies to intestines, sloughed-off skin to department stores while other poets make heavy weather of one kiss, one kick, one letter... from verbal nuances to mind-expanding imaginative leaps, her words seem freshly plucked from the minds of non-poets– that is, she makes it look easy.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-30)

Of her own writing, Duffy has said: "I'm not interested, as a poet, in words like 'plash'—[Seamus Heaney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seamus_Heaney "Seamus Heaney") words, interesting words. I like to use simple words, but in a complicated way."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-Forbes-3) She told _The Observer_: "Like the sand and the oyster, it's a creative irritant. In each poem, I'm trying to reveal a truth, so it can't have a fictional beginning."[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-31)

Duffy rose to greater prominence in UK poetry circles after her poem "Whoever She Was" won the [Poetry Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poetry_Society "Poetry Society") National Poetry Competition in 1983.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-32) In her first collection, _Standing Female Nude_ (1985), she uses the voices of outsiders, for example in the poems "[Education for Leisure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education_for_Leisure "Education for Leisure")" and "Dear Norman." Her next collection, _Feminine Gospels_ (2002), continues this vein, showing an increased interest in long narrative poems, accessible in style and often surreal in their imagery. Her 2005 publication, _[Rapture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapture\_(poetry\_collection) "Rapture (poetry collection)")_ (2005), is a series of intimate poems charting the course of a love affair, for which she won the £10,000 [T. S. Eliot Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._S._Eliot_Prize "T. S. Eliot Prize"). In 2007, she published _The Hat_, a collection of poems for children. Online copies of her poems are rare, but her poem dedicated to [U A Fanthorpe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U_A_Fanthorpe "U A Fanthorpe"), "Premonitions," is available through _The Guardian_,[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-33) and several others via _The Daily Mirror_.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-35)

### In schools

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carol_Ann_Duffy&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: In schools")]

Duffy's poems are studied in British schools at ISC, GCSE, National 5, A-level, and higher levels.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-37) In August 2008, her "Education for Leisure," a poem about violence, was removed from the GCSE [AQA Anthology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AQA_Anthology "AQA Anthology"), following a complaint about its references to [knife crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knife_legislation "Knife legislation") and a goldfish being flushed down a toilet. The poem begins: "Today I am going to kill something. Anything./I have had enough of being ignored and today/I am going to play God." The protagonist kills a fly, then a goldfish. The budgie panics and the cat hides. It ends with him, or her, or them, leaving the house with a knife. "The pavements glitter suddenly. I touch your arm."[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-Curtis-38)

According to _The Guardian_, schools were urged to destroy copies of the unedited anthology,[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-Curtis-38) though this was later denied by AQA.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-Addley-39) Duffy called the decision ridiculous. "It's an anti-violence poem," she said. "It is a plea for education rather than violence." She responded with "Mrs Schofield's GCSE", a poem about violence in other fiction, and the point of it. "Explain how poetry/pursues the human like the smitten moon/above the weeping, laughing earth ..."[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-40) The Mrs. Schofield of the title refers to Pat Schofield, an external examiner at Lutterworth College, Leicestershire, who complained about "Education for Leisure," calling it "absolutely horrendous."[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-Addley-39)

For the new National Qualifications Higher English Course in Scotland, Duffy's agents, RCW Literacy Agency, refused permission for her poem, "Originally," to be reproduced in the publicly accessible version of the paper.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-41)

### _Anthologise_ annual competition for schools

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carol_Ann_Duffy&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Anthologise annual competition for schools")]

In 2011 Duffy, spearheaded a new poetry competition for schools, named [_Anthologise_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthologise_Poetry_Competition "Anthologise Poetry Competition"). The competition is administered by the [Poetry Book Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poetry_Book_Society "Poetry Book Society") and was launched by the [Duchess of Cornwall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camilla,_Duchess_of_Cornwall "Camilla, Duchess of Cornwall") in September 2011. School students aged 11–18 from around the UK were invited to create and submit their own anthologies of published poetry. The 2011 _Anthologise_ judges were Duffy; [Gillian Clarke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gillian_Clarke "Gillian Clarke") (National Poet for Wales); [John Agard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Agard "John Agard"); [Grace Nichols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grace_Nichols "Grace Nichols") and Cambridge Professor of Children's Poetry, [Morag Styles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morag_Styles?action=edit&redlink=1 "Morag Styles (page does not exist)"). The first ever winners of _Anthologise_ were the sixth form pupils of [Monkton Combe School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monkton_Combe_School "Monkton Combe School"), [Bath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bath,_Somerset "Bath, Somerset"), with their anthology titled _The Poetry of Earth is Never Dead_, which was described by Duffy as "assured and accomplished as any anthology currently on the bookshelves."[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-42)

### Plays and songs

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carol_Ann_Duffy&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Plays and songs")]

Duffy is also a playwright, and has had plays performed at the [Liverpool Playhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_Playhouse "Liverpool Playhouse") and the [Almeida Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almeida_Theatre "Almeida Theatre") in London. Her plays include _Take My Husband_ (1982), _Cavern of Dreams_ (1984), _Little Women, Big Boys_ (1986) _Loss_ (1986), _Casanova_ (2007). Her radio credits include an adaptation of _Rapture_.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-43) Her children's collections include _Meeting Midnight_ (1999) and _The Oldest Girl in the World_ (2000). She also collaborated with the Manchester composer, [Sasha Johnson Manning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sasha_Johnson_Manning "Sasha Johnson Manning"), on _The Manchester Carols_, a series of Christmas songs that premiered in [Manchester Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_Cathedral "Manchester Cathedral") in 2007.

She also participated in the [Bush Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bush_Theatre "Bush Theatre")'s 2011 project _[Sixty-Six Books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixty-Six\_Books "Sixty-Six Books")_, for which she wrote a piece based on a book of the [King James Bible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_James_Bible "King James Bible").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-44)

A modernised adaptation of _[Everyman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everyman\_(15th-century\_play) "Everyman (15th-century play)")_ by Duffy, with [Chiwetel Ejiofor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiwetel_Ejiofor "Chiwetel Ejiofor") in the title role, was performed at the [Royal National Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Theatre "Royal National Theatre") from April to July 2015.

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carol_Ann_Duffy&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Personal life")]

At the age of 16, Duffy began a relationship with poet [Adrian Henri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrian_Henri "Adrian Henri"), living with him until 1982.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-stylist.co.uk-45) Duffy later met poet [Jackie Kay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Kay "Jackie Kay"), with whom she had a 15-year relationship.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-stylist.co.uk-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-46) During her relationship with Kay, Duffy gave birth to a daughter, Ella (born 1995), whose biological father is fellow poet [Peter Benson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Benson_(author) "Peter Benson (author)").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-stylist.co.uk-45)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-47)

Raised in her parents' Roman Catholic faith, Duffy became an [atheist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atheist "Atheist") when she was 15. However, she has spoken of the influence her religious upbringing has had on her poetry, stating: "Poetry and prayer are very similar."[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-48)

She is a [lesbian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lesbian "Lesbian").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-49)

**Dame Carol Ann Duffy** (born 23 December 1955) is a Scottish[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-Forbes-3) poet and playwright. She is a professor of contemporary poetry at [Manchester Metropolitan University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_Metropolitan_University "Manchester Metropolitan University"), and was appointed [Poet Laureate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poet_Laureate_of_the_United_Kingdom "Poet Laureate of the United Kingdom") in May 2009,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-about-4) serving in this position until her term ended in 2019. She was the first female, the first Scottish-born and the first openly lesbian poet to hold the Poet Laureate position.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-5)

Her collections include _Standing Female Nude_ (1985), winner of a [Scottish Arts Council Book Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Mortgage_Investment_Trust_Book_Awards "Scottish Mortgage Investment Trust Book Awards"); _Selling Manhattan_ (1987), which won a [Somerset Maugham Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerset_Maugham_Award "Somerset Maugham Award"); _Mean Time_ (1993), which won the [Whitbread Poetry Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costa_Book_Award_for_Poetry "Costa Book Award for Poetry"); and _[Rapture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapture\_(poetry\_collection) "Rapture (poetry collection)")_ (2005), which won the [T. S. Eliot Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._S._Eliot_Prize "T. S. Eliot Prize"). Her poems address issues such as [oppression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oppression "Oppression"), gender, and violence, in accessible language.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-EB-6)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carol_Ann_Duffy&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Carol Ann Duffy was born into a Roman Catholic family in the [Gorbals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorbals "Gorbals")[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-scottishpoetrylibrary-7) area of [Glasgow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glasgow "Glasgow"). She was the daughter of Mary (née Black) and Frank Duffy, an electrical fitter.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-Forbes-3) Her mother's parents were Irish, and her father had Irish grandparents.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-scottishpoetrylibrary-7) The eldest of five siblings, she has four brothers: Frank, Adrian, Eugene and Tim. The family moved to [Stafford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stafford "Stafford"), England, when Duffy was six years old. Her father worked for [English Electric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Electric "English Electric"). A trade unionist, he stood unsuccessfully as a parliamentary candidate for the [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK) "Labour Party (UK)") in 1983 in addition to managing [Stafford Football Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stafford_Town_F.C. "Stafford Town F.C.").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-Forbes-3)

Duffy was educated in Stafford at Saint Austin's RC Primary School (1962–1967), St. Joseph's Convent School (1967–1970), and [Stafford Girls' High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Edward_VI_High_School,_Stafford "King Edward VI High School, Stafford") (1970–1974), her literary talent encouraged by two English teachers, June Scriven at St Joseph's, and Jim Walker at Stafford Girls' High.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-Forbes-3) She was a passionate reader from an early age, and always wanted to be a writer, producing poems from the age of 11. When one of her English teachers died, she wrote:

> You sat on your desk,  
>  swinging your legs,   
>  reading a poem by Yeats   
>  to the bored girls,   
>  except my heart stumbled and blushed  
>  as it fell in love with the words and I saw the tree   
>  in the scratched old desk under my hands,   
>  heard the bird in the oak outside scribble itself on the air.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-8)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carol_Ann_Duffy&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

> Some days, although we cannot pray, a prayer  
>  utters itself. So, a woman will lift  
>  her head from the sieve of her hands and stare  
>  at the minims sung by a tree, a sudden gift.  
>   
>  Some nights, although we are faithless, the truth  
>  enters our hearts, that small familiar pain;  
>  then a man will stand stock-still, hearing his youth  
>  in the distant Latin chanting of a train.

—From "Prayer",   
_Mean Time_, Anvil, 1994[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-9)

When Duffy was 15, June Scriven sent her poems to _Outposts_, a publisher of pamphlets, where it was read by the bookseller Bernard Stone, who published some of them. When she was 16, she met [Adrian Henri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrian_Henri "Adrian Henri"), 39 at the time, one of the [Liverpool poets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_poets "Liverpool poets"), and decided she wanted to be with him; she then lived with him for 10 years until they split in 1982. "He gave me confidence," she said, "he was great. It was all poetry, very heady, and he was never faithful. He thought poets had a duty to be unfaithful."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-Winterson-10)

She applied to the [University of Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Liverpool "University of Liverpool") to be near him, and began a [philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophy "Philosophy") degree there in 1974. She had two plays performed at the [Liverpool Playhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_Playhouse "Liverpool Playhouse"), wrote a pamphlet, _Fifth Last Song_, and received an honours degree in philosophy in 1977.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-Forbes-3) She won the [National Poetry Competition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Poetry_Competition "National Poetry Competition") in 1983. She worked as poetry critic for _The Guardian_ from 1988 to 1989, and was editor of the poetry magazine, [_Ambit_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambit_(magazine) "Ambit (magazine)"). In 1996, she was appointed as a lecturer in poetry at [Manchester Metropolitan University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_Metropolitan_University "Manchester Metropolitan University"), and later became creative director of its Writing School.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-EB-6)

Duffy was a contender for the post of [Poet Laureate of the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poet_Laureate_of_the_United_Kingdom "Poet Laureate of the United Kingdom") in 1999 after the death of [Ted Hughes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Hughes "Ted Hughes"), but lost out to [Andrew Motion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Motion "Andrew Motion"). Duffy said she would not have accepted the position at that time anyway, because she was in a relationship with Scottish poet [Jackie Kay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Kay "Jackie Kay"), had a young daughter, and would not have welcomed the public attention.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-11) In the same year, she was elected as a Fellow of the [Royal Society of Literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Society_of_Literature "Royal Society of Literature").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-12)

She was appointed as Poet Laureate on 1 May 2009,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-13) when Motion's 10-year term was over. Duffy was featured on _[The South Bank Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_South\_Bank\_Show "The South Bank Show")_ with [Melvyn Bragg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melvyn_Bragg "Melvyn Bragg") in December 2009[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-14) and on 7 December she presented the [Turner Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turner_Prize "Turner Prize") to artist [Richard Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Wright_(artist) "Richard Wright (artist)").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-15)

Duffy received an Honorary Doctorate from [Heriot-Watt University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heriot-Watt_University "Heriot-Watt University") in 2009.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-16)

In 2015, Duffy was elected as an [Honorary Fellow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honorary_Fellow "Honorary Fellow") of the [British Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Academy "British Academy").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-17)

### Poet laureate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carol_Ann_Duffy&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Poet laureate")]

In her first poem as poet laureate, Duffy tackled the scandal over British [MPs' expenses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_Parliamentary_expenses_scandal "United Kingdom Parliamentary expenses scandal") in the format of a [sonnet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonnet "Sonnet").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-18) Her second, "[Last Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Post_(poem) "Last Post (poem)")", was commissioned by the BBC to mark the deaths of [Henry Allingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Allingham "Henry Allingham") and [Harry Patch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Patch "Harry Patch"), the last remaining British soldiers to fight in World War I.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-19) Her third, "The Twelve Days of Christmas 2009", addresses current events such as [species extinction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Species_extinction "Species extinction"), the [climate change conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copenhagen_United_Nations_Climate_Change_Conference "Copenhagen United Nations Climate Change Conference") in Copenhagen, the [banking crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banking_crisis "Banking crisis"), and the [war in Afghanistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_in_Afghanistan_(2001%E2%80%93present) "War in Afghanistan (2001–present)").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-20) In March 2010, she wrote "Achilles (for David Beckham)" about the [Achilles tendon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achilles_tendon "Achilles tendon") injury that left [David Beckham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Beckham "David Beckham") out of the English football team at the [2010 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_FIFA_World_Cup "2010 FIFA World Cup");[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-21) the poem was published in _[The Daily Mirror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily\_Mirror "Daily Mirror")_ and treats modern celebrity culture as a kind of mythicisation.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-22) "Silver Lining," written in April 2010, acknowledges the grounding of flights caused by the ash of the Icelandic volcano [Eyjafjallajökull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eyjafjallaj%C3%B6kull "Eyjafjallajökull").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-23) On 30 August 2010 she premièred her poem "Vigil" for the [Manchester Pride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_Pride "Manchester Pride") Candlelight Vigil in memory of [LGBTQ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBTQ "LGBTQ") people who have lost their lives to [HIV/AIDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HIV/AIDS "HIV/AIDS").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-24)

Duffy wrote a 46-line poem, "Rings," for the 2011 [wedding of Prince William and Catherine Middleton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wedding_of_Prince_William_and_Catherine_Middleton "Wedding of Prince William and Catherine Middleton"). The poem celebrates the rings found in nature and does not specifically mention the couple's names. It begins _for both to say_ and continues: "I might have raised your hand to the sky / to give you the ring surrounding the moon / or looked to twin the rings of your eyes / with mine / or added a ring to the rings of a tree / by forming a handheld circle with you, thee, / ...". She wrote the verse with Stephen Raw, a textual artist, and a signed print of the work was sent to the couple as a wedding gift.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-26) Duffy also wrote the poem "The Throne," which she composed for the 60th anniversary of [Queen Elizabeth II's coronation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronation_of_Queen_Elizabeth_II "Coronation of Queen Elizabeth II").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-27)

In _[Stylist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stylist\_(magazine) "Stylist (magazine)")_ magazine,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-Interview-28) Duffy said of becoming poet laureate: "There's no requirement. I do get asked to do things and so far I've been happy to do them." She also spoke about being appointed to the role by [Queen Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II"), saying: "She's lovely! I met her before I became poet laureate but when I was appointed I had an 'audience' with her which meant we were alone, at the palace, for the first time. We chatted about poetry. Her mother was friends with [Ted Hughes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Hughes "Ted Hughes") whose poetry I admire a lot. We spoke about his influence on me."[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-Interview-28)

Duffy stood down as laureate in May 2019.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-Guardian181027-29)

## Poetry

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carol_Ann_Duffy&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Poetry")]

### Style

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carol_Ann_Duffy&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Style")]

Duffy's work explores both everyday experience and the rich fantasy life of herself and others. In dramatizing scenes from childhood, adolescence, and adult life, she discovers moments of consolation through love, memory, and language. [Charlotte Mendelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte_Mendelson "Charlotte Mendelson") writes in _The Observer_:

> Part of Duffy's talent– besides her ear for ordinary eloquence, her gorgeous, powerful, throwaway lines, her subtlety– is her ventriloquism. Like the best of her novelist peers... she slides in and out of her characters' lives on a stream of possessions, aspirations, idioms and turns of phrase. However, she is also a time-traveller and a shape-shifter, gliding from [Troy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troy "Troy") to Hollywood, galaxies to intestines, sloughed-off skin to department stores while other poets make heavy weather of one kiss, one kick, one letter... from verbal nuances to mind-expanding imaginative leaps, her words seem freshly plucked from the minds of non-poets– that is, she makes it look easy.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-30)

Of her own writing, Duffy has said: "I'm not interested, as a poet, in words like 'plash'—[Seamus Heaney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seamus_Heaney "Seamus Heaney") words, interesting words. I like to use simple words, but in a complicated way."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-Forbes-3) She told _The Observer_: "Like the sand and the oyster, it's a creative irritant. In each poem, I'm trying to reveal a truth, so it can't have a fictional beginning."[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-31)

Duffy rose to greater prominence in UK poetry circles after her poem "Whoever She Was" won the [Poetry Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poetry_Society "Poetry Society") National Poetry Competition in 1983.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-32) In her first collection, _Standing Female Nude_ (1985), she uses the voices of outsiders, for example in the poems "[Education for Leisure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education_for_Leisure "Education for Leisure")" and "Dear Norman." Her next collection, _Feminine Gospels_ (2002), continues this vein, showing an increased interest in long narrative poems, accessible in style and often surreal in their imagery. Her 2005 publication, _[Rapture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapture\_(poetry\_collection) "Rapture (poetry collection)")_ (2005), is a series of intimate poems charting the course of a love affair, for which she won the £10,000 [T. S. Eliot Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._S._Eliot_Prize "T. S. Eliot Prize"). In 2007, she published _The Hat_, a collection of poems for children. Online copies of her poems are rare, but her poem dedicated to [U A Fanthorpe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U_A_Fanthorpe "U A Fanthorpe"), "Premonitions," is available through _The Guardian_,[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-33) and several others via _The Daily Mirror_.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-35)

### In schools

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carol_Ann_Duffy&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: In schools")]

Duffy's poems are studied in British schools at ISC, GCSE, National 5, A-level, and higher levels.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-37) In August 2008, her "Education for Leisure," a poem about violence, was removed from the GCSE [AQA Anthology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AQA_Anthology "AQA Anthology"), following a complaint about its references to [knife crime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knife_legislation "Knife legislation") and a goldfish being flushed down a toilet. The poem begins: "Today I am going to kill something. Anything./I have had enough of being ignored and today/I am going to play God." The protagonist kills a fly, then a goldfish. The budgie panics and the cat hides. It ends with him, or her, or them, leaving the house with a knife. "The pavements glitter suddenly. I touch your arm."[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-Curtis-38)

According to _The Guardian_, schools were urged to destroy copies of the unedited anthology,[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-Curtis-38) though this was later denied by AQA.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-Addley-39) Duffy called the decision ridiculous. "It's an anti-violence poem," she said. "It is a plea for education rather than violence." She responded with "Mrs Schofield's GCSE", a poem about violence in other fiction, and the point of it. "Explain how poetry/pursues the human like the smitten moon/above the weeping, laughing earth ..."[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-40) The Mrs. Schofield of the title refers to Pat Schofield, an external examiner at Lutterworth College, Leicestershire, who complained about "Education for Leisure," calling it "absolutely horrendous."[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-Addley-39)

For the new National Qualifications Higher English Course in Scotland, Duffy's agents, RCW Literacy Agency, refused permission for her poem, "Originally," to be reproduced in the publicly accessible version of the paper.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-41)

### _Anthologise_ annual competition for schools

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carol_Ann_Duffy&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Anthologise annual competition for schools")]

In 2011 Duffy, spearheaded a new poetry competition for schools, named [_Anthologise_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthologise_Poetry_Competition "Anthologise Poetry Competition"). The competition is administered by the [Poetry Book Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poetry_Book_Society "Poetry Book Society") and was launched by the [Duchess of Cornwall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camilla,_Duchess_of_Cornwall "Camilla, Duchess of Cornwall") in September 2011. School students aged 11–18 from around the UK were invited to create and submit their own anthologies of published poetry. The 2011 _Anthologise_ judges were Duffy; [Gillian Clarke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gillian_Clarke "Gillian Clarke") (National Poet for Wales); [John Agard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Agard "John Agard"); [Grace Nichols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grace_Nichols "Grace Nichols") and Cambridge Professor of Children's Poetry, [Morag Styles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morag_Styles?action=edit&redlink=1 "Morag Styles (page does not exist)"). The first ever winners of _Anthologise_ were the sixth form pupils of [Monkton Combe School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monkton_Combe_School "Monkton Combe School"), [Bath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bath,_Somerset "Bath, Somerset"), with their anthology titled _The Poetry of Earth is Never Dead_, which was described by Duffy as "assured and accomplished as any anthology currently on the bookshelves."[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-42)

### Plays and songs

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carol_Ann_Duffy&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Plays and songs")]

Duffy is also a playwright, and has had plays performed at the [Liverpool Playhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_Playhouse "Liverpool Playhouse") and the [Almeida Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almeida_Theatre "Almeida Theatre") in London. Her plays include _Take My Husband_ (1982), _Cavern of Dreams_ (1984), _Little Women, Big Boys_ (1986) _Loss_ (1986), _Casanova_ (2007). Her radio credits include an adaptation of _Rapture_.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-43) Her children's collections include _Meeting Midnight_ (1999) and _The Oldest Girl in the World_ (2000). She also collaborated with the Manchester composer, [Sasha Johnson Manning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sasha_Johnson_Manning "Sasha Johnson Manning"), on _The Manchester Carols_, a series of Christmas songs that premiered in [Manchester Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_Cathedral "Manchester Cathedral") in 2007.

She also participated in the [Bush Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bush_Theatre "Bush Theatre")'s 2011 project _[Sixty-Six Books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixty-Six\_Books "Sixty-Six Books")_, for which she wrote a piece based on a book of the [King James Bible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_James_Bible "King James Bible").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-44)

A modernised adaptation of _[Everyman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everyman\_(15th-century\_play) "Everyman (15th-century play)")_ by Duffy, with [Chiwetel Ejiofor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiwetel_Ejiofor "Chiwetel Ejiofor") in the title role, was performed at the [Royal National Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_National_Theatre "Royal National Theatre") from April to July 2015.

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Carol_Ann_Duffy&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Personal life")]

At the age of 16, Duffy began a relationship with poet [Adrian Henri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrian_Henri "Adrian Henri"), living with him until 1982.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-stylist.co.uk-45) Duffy later met poet [Jackie Kay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Kay "Jackie Kay"), with whom she had a 15-year relationship.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-stylist.co.uk-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-46) During her relationship with Kay, Duffy gave birth to a daughter, Ella (born 1995), whose biological father is fellow poet [Peter Benson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Benson_(author) "Peter Benson (author)").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-stylist.co.uk-45)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-47)

Raised in her parents' Roman Catholic faith, Duffy became an [atheist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atheist "Atheist") when she was 15. However, she has spoken of the influence her religious upbringing has had on her poetry, stating: "Poetry and prayer are very similar."[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-48)

She is a [lesbian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lesbian "Lesbian").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carol_Ann_Duffy#cite_note-49)

**Barbara Guest**, _née_**Barbara Ann Pinson** (September 6, 1920 – February 15, 2006), was an American [poet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poet "Poet") and [prose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prose "Prose") stylist. Guest first gained recognition as a member of the first generation [New York School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_School_(art) "New York School (art)") of poetry. Guest wrote more than 15 books of poetry spanning sixty years of writing. In 1999, she was awarded the [Frost Medal for Lifetime Achievement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poetry_Society_of_America#Awards "Poetry Society of America") by the [Poetry Society of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poetry_Society_of_America "Poetry Society of America").

Guest also wrote [art criticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_criticism "Art criticism"), essays, a novel, biography, [plays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Play_(theatre) "Play (theatre)"), and other prose pieces since collected in _Meditations: The Assorted Prose of Barbara Guest_. Her [collages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collage "Collage") appeared on the covers of several of her books of poetry. She was also well known for her biography of the poet [H.D.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H.D. "H.D."), _Herself Defined: The Poet H.D. and Her World_ (1984).

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Barbara_Guest&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Born in [Wilmington, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilmington,_North_Carolina "Wilmington, North Carolina") and raised in [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), Guest attended [UCLA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Los_Angeles "University of California, Los Angeles"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Guest#cite_note-1) and then earned a [B.A.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") in General Curriculum-Humanities in 1943 at [UC Berkeley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Berkeley "University of California, Berkeley"). She worked as an editorial associate at _[ARTnews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARTnews "ARTnews")_ magazine from 1951 to 1959.

## Poetry

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Barbara_Guest&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Poetry")]

Barbara Guest wrote more than 15 books of poetry spanning sixty years of writing. "Her poems begin in the midst of action," wrote [Peter Gizzi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gizzi "Peter Gizzi") in his introduction to a collection of her work, "but their angle of perception is oblique."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Guest#cite_note-2) Her poems are known for their abstract quality, vivid language, and intellectualism. She believed that the subject of the poem finds itself through the writing of the poem and through the poet's imagination. "Disturbing the conventional relations of subjects and objects, of reality and imagination, is one of Guest's signature gestures," noted Gizzi.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Guest#cite_note-3)

Among her most well-known poems are ["Parachutes, My Love, Could Carry Us Higher," (MP3)](https://media.sas.upenn.edu/pennsound/authors/Guest/Linebreak/Guest-Barbara_04_Parachutes_LINEbreak_NY_1995.mp3)["Wild Gardens Overlooked by Night Lights, (MP3)"](https://media.sas.upenn.edu/pennsound/authors/Guest/Linebreak/Guest-Barbara_11_Wild-Gardens-Overlooked-by-Night-Lights_LINEbreak_NY_1995.mp3)["Roses,"](http://www.poetryfoundation.org/poem/237242) and ["Photographs."](http://www.poetryfoundation.org/poem/172231)

## Quotes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Barbara_Guest&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Quotes")]

> The subject matter finds itself...You find the subject as you proceed with (writing) the poem.

—Barbara Guest, _Interview on LINEBreak with Charles Bernstein. 1995_

> Poetry is where the concrete object is bathed in a new atmosphere lifted out of itself to become a fiction. The poet is not there only to share a poetic communication but to stimulate an imaginative speculation on the nature of reality.

—Barbara Guest, _Lecture titled "How I Got Out of Poetry and into Prose." 1992._

> The poet wishes to align the contents of the poem with the vision which directs it. When this occurs, we say of a poem that it has wings. It is possible that words may occur in a fixed space and sequences so that they are called words of a poem. We say this poem is made of words. It is true many poems are constructed solely of words. These are the words that sit on paper without vision. We have all read these poems and we know after we have read them, we feel curiously bereft. Our expectations of enoblement by the poem have been disappointed by the lackluster condition of the poem. We decide that this poem is not very inspired. And what do we mean by this? We desired inspiration that the poem contained within it, the spirit of poetry. We have learned that words are only utensils. They are inorganic unless there is a spirit within the poem, to elevate it, to give it wings so that the poem may soar above the page and enter our consciousness where we may, if we wish, give it a long life.

—Barbara Guest, _Lecture titled "How I Got Out of Poetry and into Prose." 1992._

> (Imagination) is something fluid which can twist itself into a poem.

—Barbara Guest, _Interview on LINEBreak with Charles Bernstein. 1995_

"To speak with Barbara Guest about poetry was always to be in the presence of a fiercely uncompromised vision of the art and its obligations. Her insights continually astonished me. They were beholden to no one. And the work itself, of a lyric intelligence entirely her own. For whatever reasons, and I can sadly imagine many, it has not received its full due, but it will. The music insists."
[Michael Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Palmer_(poet) "Michael Palmer (poet)")[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Guest#cite_note-4)

**Barbara Guest**, _née_**Barbara Ann Pinson** (September 6, 1920 – February 15, 2006), was an American [poet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poet "Poet") and [prose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prose "Prose") stylist. Guest first gained recognition as a member of the first generation [New York School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_School_(art) "New York School (art)") of poetry. Guest wrote more than 15 books of poetry spanning sixty years of writing. In 1999, she was awarded the [Frost Medal for Lifetime Achievement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poetry_Society_of_America#Awards "Poetry Society of America") by the [Poetry Society of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poetry_Society_of_America "Poetry Society of America").

Guest also wrote [art criticism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_criticism "Art criticism"), essays, a novel, biography, [plays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Play_(theatre) "Play (theatre)"), and other prose pieces since collected in _Meditations: The Assorted Prose of Barbara Guest_. Her [collages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collage "Collage") appeared on the covers of several of her books of poetry. She was also well known for her biography of the poet [H.D.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H.D. "H.D."), _Herself Defined: The Poet H.D. and Her World_ (1984).

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Barbara_Guest&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Born in [Wilmington, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilmington,_North_Carolina "Wilmington, North Carolina") and raised in [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), Guest attended [UCLA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Los_Angeles "University of California, Los Angeles"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Guest#cite_note-1) and then earned a [B.A.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") in General Curriculum-Humanities in 1943 at [UC Berkeley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_California,_Berkeley "University of California, Berkeley"). She worked as an editorial associate at _[ARTnews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARTnews "ARTnews")_ magazine from 1951 to 1959.

## Poetry

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Barbara_Guest&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Poetry")]

Barbara Guest wrote more than 15 books of poetry spanning sixty years of writing. "Her poems begin in the midst of action," wrote [Peter Gizzi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gizzi "Peter Gizzi") in his introduction to a collection of her work, "but their angle of perception is oblique."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Guest#cite_note-2) Her poems are known for their abstract quality, vivid language, and intellectualism. She believed that the subject of the poem finds itself through the writing of the poem and through the poet's imagination. "Disturbing the conventional relations of subjects and objects, of reality and imagination, is one of Guest's signature gestures," noted Gizzi.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Guest#cite_note-3)

Among her most well-known poems are ["Parachutes, My Love, Could Carry Us Higher," (MP3)](https://media.sas.upenn.edu/pennsound/authors/Guest/Linebreak/Guest-Barbara_04_Parachutes_LINEbreak_NY_1995.mp3)["Wild Gardens Overlooked by Night Lights, (MP3)"](https://media.sas.upenn.edu/pennsound/authors/Guest/Linebreak/Guest-Barbara_11_Wild-Gardens-Overlooked-by-Night-Lights_LINEbreak_NY_1995.mp3)["Roses,"](http://www.poetryfoundation.org/poem/237242) and ["Photographs."](http://www.poetryfoundation.org/poem/172231)

## Quotes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Barbara_Guest&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Quotes")]

> The subject matter finds itself...You find the subject as you proceed with (writing) the poem.

—Barbara Guest, _Interview on LINEBreak with Charles Bernstein. 1995_

> Poetry is where the concrete object is bathed in a new atmosphere lifted out of itself to become a fiction. The poet is not there only to share a poetic communication but to stimulate an imaginative speculation on the nature of reality.

—Barbara Guest, _Lecture titled "How I Got Out of Poetry and into Prose." 1992._

> The poet wishes to align the contents of the poem with the vision which directs it. When this occurs, we say of a poem that it has wings. It is possible that words may occur in a fixed space and sequences so that they are called words of a poem. We say this poem is made of words. It is true many poems are constructed solely of words. These are the words that sit on paper without vision. We have all read these poems and we know after we have read them, we feel curiously bereft. Our expectations of enoblement by the poem have been disappointed by the lackluster condition of the poem. We decide that this poem is not very inspired. And what do we mean by this? We desired inspiration that the poem contained within it, the spirit of poetry. We have learned that words are only utensils. They are inorganic unless there is a spirit within the poem, to elevate it, to give it wings so that the poem may soar above the page and enter our consciousness where we may, if we wish, give it a long life.

—Barbara Guest, _Lecture titled "How I Got Out of Poetry and into Prose." 1992._

> (Imagination) is something fluid which can twist itself into a poem.

—Barbara Guest, _Interview on LINEBreak with Charles Bernstein. 1995_

"To speak with Barbara Guest about poetry was always to be in the presence of a fiercely uncompromised vision of the art and its obligations. Her insights continually astonished me. They were beholden to no one. And the work itself, of a lyric intelligence entirely her own. For whatever reasons, and I can sadly imagine many, it has not received its full due, but it will. The music insists."
[Michael Palmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Palmer_(poet) "Michael Palmer (poet)")[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_Guest#cite_note-4)

# Marie Howe

[http://www.mariehowe.com](http://www.mariehowe.com/)

B.1950

Share

![Image 6: Image of Marie Howe](https://cdn.poetryfoundation.org/cdn-cgi/image/w=2292,h=1528,q=80/content/images/17fba72363b54e7a9ddac96522ddee9c173ae908.jpeg)

Brad Fowler. Courtesy of Blue Flower Arts.

Born in Rochester, New York, Marie Howe attended Sacred Heart Convent School and the University of Windsor. She earned an MFA from Columbia University, where she studied with [Stanley Kunitz](http://www.poetryfoundation.org/archive/poet.html?id=3869), whom she refers to as “my true teacher.”  
  
Her first collection, _The Good Thief_ (1988), was chosen for the National Poetry Series by [Margaret Atwood](http://www.poetryfoundation.org/archive/poet.html?id=252), who praised Howe’s “poems of obsession that transcend their own dark roots.” In that collection, Howe’s oracular yet self-doubting speakers often voice their concerns through Biblical and mythical allusions. Kunitz, on selecting the book for the Lavan Younger Poets Prize from the American Academy of Poets, observed, “Her long, deep-breathing lines address the mysteries of flesh and spirit, in terms accessible only to a woman who is very much of our time and yet still in touch with the sacred.”  
  
In 1989, Howe’s brother John died of an AIDS-related illness. As Howe states in an _AGNI_ interview, “John’s living and dying changed my aesthetic completely.” _What the Living Do_ (1997), an elegy to John, was praised by _Publishers Weekly_ as one of the five best poetry collections of the year. Stripping her poems of metaphor, Howe composed the collection as a transparent, accessible documentary of loss.  
  
In _The Kingdom of Ordinary Time_ (2008), Howe distanced herself from the personal narrative and returned to, as she describes in the _AGNI_ interview, her “obsess[ion] with the metaphysical, the spiritual dimensions of life as they present themselves in this world.” In these poems Howe “makes metaphor matter and material metaphysical,” according to [Brenda Shaughnessy](http://www.poetryfoundation.org/archive/poet.html?id=98909) in _Publishers Weekly_. Howe’s fourth book of poetry is _Magdalene_(2017). _New and Selected Poems_ (2024) was awarded the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry.

Howe has taught at Sarah Lawrence College, Columbia University, and NYU. She coedited (with Michael Klein) the essay anthology _In the Company of My Solitude: American Writing from the AIDS Pandemic_ (1994). She has received fellowships from the Bunting Institute at Radcliffe College, the National Endowment for the Arts, the Guggenheim Foundation, the Academy of American Poets, and the Fine Arts Work Center in Provincetown. She was the Poet Laureate of New York State from 2012 to 2014.She is the poet in residence at The Cathedral Church of St. John the Divine and a chancellor of the Academy of American Poets. Howe lives in New York City.

# Marie Howe

[http://www.mariehowe.com](http://www.mariehowe.com/)

B.1950

Share

![Image 6: Image of Marie Howe](https://cdn.poetryfoundation.org/cdn-cgi/image/w=2292,h=1528,q=80/content/images/17fba72363b54e7a9ddac96522ddee9c173ae908.jpeg)

Brad Fowler. Courtesy of Blue Flower Arts.

Born in Rochester, New York, Marie Howe attended Sacred Heart Convent School and the University of Windsor. She earned an MFA from Columbia University, where she studied with [Stanley Kunitz](http://www.poetryfoundation.org/archive/poet.html?id=3869), whom she refers to as “my true teacher.”  
  
Her first collection, _The Good Thief_ (1988), was chosen for the National Poetry Series by [Margaret Atwood](http://www.poetryfoundation.org/archive/poet.html?id=252), who praised Howe’s “poems of obsession that transcend their own dark roots.” In that collection, Howe’s oracular yet self-doubting speakers often voice their concerns through Biblical and mythical allusions. Kunitz, on selecting the book for the Lavan Younger Poets Prize from the American Academy of Poets, observed, “Her long, deep-breathing lines address the mysteries of flesh and spirit, in terms accessible only to a woman who is very much of our time and yet still in touch with the sacred.”  
  
In 1989, Howe’s brother John died of an AIDS-related illness. As Howe states in an _AGNI_ interview, “John’s living and dying changed my aesthetic completely.” _What the Living Do_ (1997), an elegy to John, was praised by _Publishers Weekly_ as one of the five best poetry collections of the year. Stripping her poems of metaphor, Howe composed the collection as a transparent, accessible documentary of loss.  
  
In _The Kingdom of Ordinary Time_ (2008), Howe distanced herself from the personal narrative and returned to, as she describes in the _AGNI_ interview, her “obsess[ion] with the metaphysical, the spiritual dimensions of life as they present themselves in this world.” In these poems Howe “makes metaphor matter and material metaphysical,” according to [Brenda Shaughnessy](http://www.poetryfoundation.org/archive/poet.html?id=98909) in _Publishers Weekly_. Howe’s fourth book of poetry is _Magdalene_(2017). _New and Selected Poems_ (2024) was awarded the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry.

Howe has taught at Sarah Lawrence College, Columbia University, and NYU. She coedited (with Michael Klein) the essay anthology _In the Company of My Solitude: American Writing from the AIDS Pandemic_ (1994). She has received fellowships from the Bunting Institute at Radcliffe College, the National Endowment for the Arts, the Guggenheim Foundation, the Academy of American Poets, and the Fine Arts Work Center in Provincetown. She was the Poet Laureate of New York State from 2012 to 2014.She is the poet in residence at The Cathedral Church of St. John the Divine and a chancellor of the Academy of American Poets. Howe lives in New York City.

# Kay Ryan

B.1945

Share

![Image 6: Kay Ryan](https://cdn.poetryfoundation.org/cdn-cgi/image/w=2292,h=1500,q=80/content/images/0d521b733b1b1e9ea3eb88c926ca72d4dab501cf.jpeg)

Don Usner

Born in California in 1945 and acknowledged as one of the most original voices in the contemporary landscape, Kay Ryan is the author of several books of poetry, including _Flamingo Watching_ (2006), _The Niagara River_ (2005), and _Say Uncle_ (2000). Her book _The Best of It: New and Selected Poems_ (2010) won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry.

Ryan’s tightly compressed, rhythmically dense poetry is often compared to that of Emily Dickinson and Marianne Moore; however, Ryan’s often barbed wit and unique facility with “recombinant” rhyme has earned her the status of one of the great living American poets, and led to her appointment as U.S. Poet Laureate in 2008. She held the position for two terms, using the appointment to champion community colleges like the one in Marin County, California where she and her partner Carol Adair taught for over thirty years. In an interview with the _Washington City Paper_ at the end of tenure, Ryan called herself a “whistle-blower” who “advocated for much underpraised and underfunded community colleges across the nation.”  
  
 Ryan’s surprising laureateship capped years of outsider-status in the poetry world. Her quizzical, philosophical, often mordant poetry is a product of years of thought. Ryan has said that her poems do not start with imagery or sound, but rather develop “the way an oyster does, with an aggravation.” Critic Meghan O’Rourke has written of her work: “Each poem twists around and back upon its argument like a river retracing its path; they are didactic in spirit, but a bedrock wit supports them.” “Sharks’ Teeth” displays that meandering approach to her subject matter, which, Ryan says, “gives my poems a coolness. I can touch things that are very hot because I’ve given them some distance.”  
  
 Kay Ryan is the recipient of several major awards, including fellowships from the John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation, the National Endowment for the Arts, the Ingram Merrill Foundation, and the Guggenheim Foundation. She has received the Union League Poetry Prize and the Maurice English Poetry Award, as well as the Ruth Lilly Poetry Prize. Since 2006 she has served as a Chancellor of the Academy of American Poets.

# Kay Ryan

B.1945

Share

![Image 6: Kay Ryan](https://cdn.poetryfoundation.org/cdn-cgi/image/w=2292,h=1500,q=80/content/images/0d521b733b1b1e9ea3eb88c926ca72d4dab501cf.jpeg)

Don Usner

Born in California in 1945 and acknowledged as one of the most original voices in the contemporary landscape, Kay Ryan is the author of several books of poetry, including _Flamingo Watching_ (2006), _The Niagara River_ (2005), and _Say Uncle_ (2000). Her book _The Best of It: New and Selected Poems_ (2010) won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry.

Ryan’s tightly compressed, rhythmically dense poetry is often compared to that of Emily Dickinson and Marianne Moore; however, Ryan’s often barbed wit and unique facility with “recombinant” rhyme has earned her the status of one of the great living American poets, and led to her appointment as U.S. Poet Laureate in 2008. She held the position for two terms, using the appointment to champion community colleges like the one in Marin County, California where she and her partner Carol Adair taught for over thirty years. In an interview with the _Washington City Paper_ at the end of tenure, Ryan called herself a “whistle-blower” who “advocated for much underpraised and underfunded community colleges across the nation.”  
  
 Ryan’s surprising laureateship capped years of outsider-status in the poetry world. Her quizzical, philosophical, often mordant poetry is a product of years of thought. Ryan has said that her poems do not start with imagery or sound, but rather develop “the way an oyster does, with an aggravation.” Critic Meghan O’Rourke has written of her work: “Each poem twists around and back upon its argument like a river retracing its path; they are didactic in spirit, but a bedrock wit supports them.” “Sharks’ Teeth” displays that meandering approach to her subject matter, which, Ryan says, “gives my poems a coolness. I can touch things that are very hot because I’ve given them some distance.”  
  
 Kay Ryan is the recipient of several major awards, including fellowships from the John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation, the National Endowment for the Arts, the Ingram Merrill Foundation, and the Guggenheim Foundation. She has received the Union League Poetry Prize and the Maurice English Poetry Award, as well as the Ruth Lilly Poetry Prize. Since 2006 she has served as a Chancellor of the Academy of American Poets.
